Once other arguments determine all parameters, substituted parameter types provide context to those expressions. This process does not reorder evaluation.
fn count[T: Shareable](values: List[T]) -> Int: return 0 let known = count[Int](values: []) # Rejected: the empty list does not determine T. let unknown = count(values: [])Generic data constructors follow the same field/payload inference rule, but an expected data application may supply their type arguments before field checking. Thus let box: Box[Int] = Box(value: 1) is valid. A unique complete application must result; a constructor cannot invent an unused type parameter.
Body checking and well-formedness# A generic body is checked once against declared bounds. An unconstrained T cannot be compared with ==, used as a map key, or called through a contract operation. Bounds expose only their declared properties.
# Rejected at declaration: missing Equal bound. fn unchecked_same[T](left: T, right: T) -> Bool: return left == right type Keys[T: Shareable & Hashable]: values: Set[T]Every nested application must satisfy its bounds under enclosing generic assumptions. Omitting the bounds from Keys is rejected even if all later uses happen to supply Int.
The same rule checks a generic implementation once under its inherited parameters and bounds. Its method bodies cannot rely on properties absent from the inherited bounds. Matching the receiver determines the implementation arguments; all implementation bounds must hold before its operations or views are available. Bounds may restrict a single implementation’s availability, but are ignored when rejecting overlapping implementations. A concrete implementation cannot specialize a pair already covered by a generic block.
Finite recursive applications# Recursive declarations follow layout rules . Separately, the compiler requires a finite regular family of recursive generic applications. Along a recursive generic cycle, arguments preserve the original parameters one-to-one in their original positions. Tree[T: Shareable] with children: List[Tree[T]] is allowed. Substituting concrete arguments, reordering them, or expanding them on a recursive cycle is rejected; Grow[T] containing List[Grow[List[T]]] would create an infinite application family. This regularity check follows recursive type references even through function signatures or contracts: an indirect runtime representation does not permit infinitely expanding static instantiations.
The same finite-application requirement covers generic function calls and specialized function values. Follow specialization dependencies through the whole module graph; on a recursive function cycle, the composed substitution must preserve the starting function’s type parameters one-to-one in their original positions. Nonrecursive calls may construct different type arguments. Reject expanding recursive specialization before Go emission, even when the recursive call is unreachable at runtime. This prevents both an infinite monomorphization worklist and generic recursion that the Go backend cannot represent.
fn repeat[T: Shareable](value: T) -> Never: return repeat[T](value: value) # Regular specialization; allowed. fn grow[T: Shareable](value: T) -> Never: return grow[List[T]](value: [value]) # Rejected: expanding specialization.Apply the check to mutual recursion and references such as grow[List[T]] stored as function values, not only direct self-calls. Include generic implementation method calls and bound methods in specialization dependencies under their inherited receiver parameters. Generated-code compilation errors are not a substitute for a source diagnostic.
Built-in requirements# Collections require shareable contents. Map keys and set elements additionally require hashing. See equality and hashing for the relationship between these properties.
Shareable is a compiler-defined bound derived from eligible immutable components and shared contract views, or declared by audited native implementations. It is not an operation contract or a source implementation target. Function types do not satisfy it, so records with function fields cannot derive sharing. The separate callable sharing rules govern closures and generic forwarding. Sharing does not register cleanup or extend a resource’s open lifetime.
Previous: Operation contracts · Next: Type compatibility and expected types

title: Type compatibility and expected types
content:
Type compatibility and expected types# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index The compiler uses the same compatibility rules for annotations, assignment, arguments, returns, constructor fields, and collection elements. An expression is assignable to an expected type when its type is exactly that type, except that an expression of Never is assignable wherever control cannot produce a value. This exception does not change function-type identity or allow return-type covariance.
Exact and nominal identity# Type form Identity and compatibility Built-in Fixed compiler or standard identity Record or alternative Defining module, declaration, and ordered type arguments; matching fields or cases do not establish compatibility Contract view Nominal contract application, plus whether it is plain or shared; conversions are explicit Generic application Exact declaration and every ordered argument; List[Int] and List[Float] are distinct Function Exact parameter labels, declaration order, parameter types, and result type; no variance or label/order adaptation Caller-written argument order affects evaluation without changing function identity. A generic bound grants properties, not subtyping. Shared/plain arguments remain distinct during inference; List[Contract] fails its element bound, while List[Contract & Shareable] may satisfy it.
Type positions use ordinary name resolution . A value shadowing a type name causes an error, not a second lookup in a hidden namespace. Unqualified cases follow alternative lookup ; expected types cannot override a lexical binding or choose an ambiguous case.
Shareable, Equal, and Hashable are compiler bounds , not standalone value types. The only value-type refinement is Contract & Shareable; other intersections and refinements are rejected.
fn identity(value: Int) -> Int: return value let exact: fn(value: Int) -> Int = identity # Rejected: amount differs from value. let relabeled: fn(amount: Int) -> Int = identityThere are no implicit numeric conversions, optional wrapping/unwrapping, result wrapping, structural record conversions, unions, or nullable references. An integer literal has type Int even under an expected Float; use the explicit conversion API . The type checker does not choose an arbitrary common type for incompatible values.
Propagating context# An explicit local annotation, assignment target, declared return type, substituted parameter type, record field type, or alternative payload type supplies an expected type to its expression. Expected types propagate through parentheses and recursively into list elements and constructor fields/payloads. They supply missing type arguments for uniquely resolved data constructors such as none, ok, and error. They do not choose between globally ambiguous unqualified constructor names or change independently determined expression types.
type Input: names: List[Optional[String]] let input = Input(names: [none, some(value: "Ada")]) let nested: List[List[Int]] = [[], [1]] let success: Result[Int, String] = ok(value: 1) let failure: Result[Int, String] = error(cause: "unavailable") # Rejected: the result error type cannot be inferred from ok's payload. let incomplete = ok(value: 1)A context-dependent expression without enough information is rejected, rather than receiving a dynamic or implicit unknown type. Thus bare unannotated none, [], and ok(value: 1) are incomplete; some(value: 1) completely determines Optional[Int]. For a nonempty list, independently typed elements can determine context for the remaining elements; [none, some(value: 1)] is List[Optional[Int]]. If independently typed elements disagree, the list is rejected.
Context flows through the constructors, literals, and parentheses listed above; it does not flow backward through operators or prefix try. Operator operands and a try operand must determine their own types before the enclosing expression is checked. In particular, an expected Int for try does not invent a Result error type from the enclosing function’s error type.
fn known() -> Result[Int, String]: let number: Int = try Result[Int, String].ok(value: 1) return ok(value: number) fn unknown() -> Result[Int, String]: # Rejected: the try operand's error type is undetermined. let number: Int = try ok(value: 1) return ok(value: number)Similarly, an expected Bool cannot make [] == [] well typed; neither operand determines a list element type. Explicitly qualify or annotate operands when their types would otherwise be incomplete.
Never operands use the operator candidate rules . Those rules select a required operand type locally; they do not infer it backward from an expected result.
Generic function inference uses supplied argument types only, as specified in generics . An expected return type does not infer missing function type arguments. A generic function value must be explicitly specialized before an expected function type can check it. Anonymous functions still require their own explicit parameter/result types.
Validation boundaries# Every declaration’s referenced types must resolve and every application must satisfy arity and bounds. Generic bodies are checked under declared bounds. Public signatures satisfy public type visibility , and recursive concrete layouts satisfy guarded recursion . These checks precede lowering and do not rely on Go’s structural interfaces or implicit assignments.
Runtime cancellation and resource closed-state errors do not alter static assignability. Their separate contracts remain governed by the existing runtime and reference chapters.
Previous: Generics and bounds · Next: Declarations and calls

title: Functions
content:
Functions# Core language guide · Design index Functions make inputs and outputs explicit. Learn declaration and call rules first, then use functions as values and account for the values a closure captures.
Concept What you will learn Declarations and calls Write explicit signatures and evaluate arguments in source order. Function values and closures Pass functions as values and understand snapshot captures and resource references.

title: Declarations and calls
content:
Declarations and calls# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A function declares its inputs and output. The body performs its work in source order and returns a value through return.
fn decrement(value: Int) -> Int: return value - 1 let remaining = decrement(value: 3)Function parameters and return types are explicit; local annotations are optional. The caller can infer remaining as Int from the function’s declared return type.
Declarations and resolution# Named functions are module declarations or operations inside an impl. Nested named function declarations are rejected; use an anonymous function bound to a local instead. Every parameter has a unique name and an explicit type, and every function has an explicit result type, including Unit.
The compiler collects module declaration names and signatures before checking bodies. A function can call a later declaration, and ordinary and mutual function recursion are allowed. Duplicate module names and overloaded declarations are rejected. Generic function declarations and applications follow generics .
Parameters belong to the function body’s lexical scope. A local declaration cannot reuse a parameter’s name in that same scope. Each branch, match arm, and loop body creates a nested scope; nested scopes may shadow an outer name.
Argument names# Every supplied function argument must use name: value, including calls with a single argument. The name identifies the declared parameter. An unnamed argument is a compile error.
fn reduce(amount: Int, deduction: Int) -> Int: return amount - deduction let remaining = reduce(amount: 10, deduction: 3)The rule applies to ordinary functions, methods, function values, and concurrency library APIs. Constructors name their fields, including some(value: ...), ok(value: ...), and error(cause: ...). A call with no supplied arguments uses ().
parallel receives an ordered pack of zero-argument functions through tasks: [first, second], with options such as timeout: 2.seconds supplied by name. Its heterogeneous results are specified in parallel operations .
Match payload bindings such as some(value): are patterns, rather than calls; see pattern matching .
Source declarations cannot define default or optional parameters, positional arguments, variadic parameters, or argument spreading. An Optional[T] source parameter is still required: callers explicitly supply none when absent. Existing trusted library API contracts may explicitly permit omitted named arguments; that permission does not follow from an Optional value type. Unknown, duplicate, and missing required argument names are compile errors. Supplied values must be compatible with the declared parameter types under type compatibility ; labels do not authorize numeric or contract conversions.
Collections as arguments# To accept a variable number of values, declare an ordinary list parameter:
fn sum(values: List[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return total let total = sum(values: [1, 2, 3]) let empty = sum(values: [])The named argument supplies one immutable list. An existing List[Int] can be passed as sum(values: existing_values). The parameter is required even for an empty list. Function values use the ordinary type fn(values: List[Int]) -> Int, and multiple list parameters need no additional call syntax.
See collections for list literals and element requirements.
Evaluation order# Execution and argument evaluation follow source order. When arguments contain calls, those calls run in the order written before the outer function receives their results. Named arguments do not reorder execution to match the parameter declaration.
Evaluate the callable expression, including a method receiver, once before its arguments. Then evaluate argument expressions from left to right in their written order. Arrange the resulting values into declaration order only after evaluation. A failed or nonreturning expression prevents all later arguments and the outer invocation from running. Constructor fields follow the same rule.
This also matters for concurrency APIs : argument preparation and closure creation happen in the caller before any operation starts.
Unit and Never# unit is the single value of Unit. A Unit function may use return, return unit, or fall through the end of its body. Other functions must return a compatible value on every reachable normal exit; bare return and reachable fallthrough are compile errors. There is no implicit return of a block’s final expression.
fn check_positive(value: Int) -> Unit: assert value > 0 fn missing_value() -> Int: return panic(message: "Required value is missing")panic has type fn(message: String) -> Never. Never has no values: a Never expression cannot complete normally and is accepted where any value type is expected. This expression rule does not make List[Never] compatible with List[Int] or change function-type identity.
Return completeness uses a conservative control-flow check:
Construct Reachable normal exits return or evaluation of Never None if without else Branch exits plus a path past the statement if with else or exhaustive match The combined exits of all branches or arms for or while with a condition other than literal true A possible exit, because the body may not execute Literal while true Only a reachable break targeting that loop A nested function’s return or nested loop’s break cannot exit the enclosing function or loop. The check uses no additional constant folding.
Expression evaluation also has no normal successor when a necessarily evaluated subexpression cannot complete. This includes callable/receiver preparation, arguments, constructor fields, list elements, interpolation expressions, unary operands, and both operands of a non-short-circuit operator. A right-hand operand of and or or alone does not remove the possible exit, because it may be skipped; their left operand is always required. Creating a function value does not execute its body. Track evaluation separately from result typing: 1 + panic(message: "stop") has type Int under the operator rules , but cannot complete normally. A failed initializer accordingly prevents the following statement from being reachable.
fn incomplete(active: Bool) -> Int: if active: return 1 # Rejected: the false path reaches the end without returning Int.Unreachable statements remain subject to parsing, name resolution, and type checking, but do not add reachable exits. A Never function must have no reachable normal return or fallthrough. A bare call may be used as a statement and its result discarded; non-call expressions cannot be standalone statements.
Calls that suspend# A potentially blocking library call suspends the current lightweight task. It does not implicitly start another task. There are no async declarations or await annotations.
Manuscript has one function kind. Sequential code remains sequential when a library operation suspends; explicit concurrent execution is specified in concurrency .
For functions used as data and the rules for captured values, continue with function values and closures .
Previous: Type compatibility and expected types · Next: Function values and closures

title: Function values and closures
content:
Function values and closures# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Functions are ordinary values. Anonymous functions use fn, and function types use fn(value: T) -> U. A closure retains the values it uses from its surrounding scope; there is no consuming function kind.
fn apply(value: Int, transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int) -> Int: return transform(value: value) let offset = 1 let decrement = fn(value: Int) -> Int: return value - offset let result = apply(value: 3, transform: decrement)Function types retain parameter names, so calls through values use named arguments. Calls have the same suspension and evaluation rules as declared functions.
Function type compatibility# Parameter names, declaration order, parameter types, and result type are all part of function-type identity. Compatibility is invariant: a different label, reordered signature, or different result type requires an explicit adapter function. Caller-written argument order may vary without changing the function’s declared type.
fn subtract_one(amount: Int) -> Int: return amount - 1 fn adapt() -> Unit: # Rejected: amount and value are different function-type labels. let invalid: fn(value: Int) -> Int = subtract_one let renamed = fn(value: Int) -> Int: return subtract_one(amount: value) let result = apply(value: 3, transform: renamed)The rejected binding is a negative example; removing it leaves a valid function. Anonymous functions require explicit parameter and result types and an indented body, exactly as specified in the grammar . An annotation on the receiving variable does not omit those signatures. A generic function must be instantiated before it is stored as a value; identity[Int] is a function value, while a bare polymorphic identity is not. Bound method values have the operation’s function type with the receiver already bound and excluded from the parameter list.
An anonymous function forms its own function boundary for return, try, break, and continue. Its control-flow exits cannot exit the containing function or loop. Capture and sharing behavior remains governed by the separate contracts below.
Snapshot captures# A closure snapshots each referenced local binding when created, including a var’s current value. Later reassignment of that local does not change the snapshot. Assigning to a captured outer local is a compile error; shared mutable local cells are not implicit. Shared mutable state is accessed through synchronized services.
Immutable data is retained by value/reference as appropriate for its representation. A service or resource capture retains a reference to the same object, not a deep copy of the object’s state. Bound methods retain their receiver under the same rules. Retained environments survive through garbage collection; there is no move, borrowed capture, or automatic cleanup on closure invocation/discard.
Resource captures# with file = try files.open(path: "data.txt"): let reader = fn() -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError]: return file.read(max_bytes: 4096) callbacks.register(handler: reader) # A later callback invocation reports IoError.Closed.The acquisition fragment belongs to a function returning Result[U, IoError]; callbacks is an explicitly supplied registration service. The standard acquisition retains File & Shareable, so concurrent callback use can preserve the receiver’s sharing proof.
Capturing a resource does not extend its open lifetime or cancel its with cleanup. Resource methods detect closed state at runtime. This applies equally to resources passed through explicit parameters or retained in records.
Concurrent invocation# Concurrency APIs accept ordinary functions with a proved safe captured environment. Local copies retain that proof; storage, generic forwarding, and source function boundaries erase it. The exact boundaries are in function sharing . A safely shared resource can still be closed before invocation.
Capture request-data snapshots and application services for background work, then acquire job resources within that operation. parallel joins before returning, so an enclosing with remains active while its operations run, unless the resource is explicitly closed elsewhere.
These examples use inferred captures. An explicit capture-list syntax has not been selected and is not required by this design. See parallel , background services , and reference sharing .
Previous: Declarations and calls · Next: Conditionals

title: Control flow
content:
Control flow# Core language guide · Design index Control flow consists of if / else, match, for / in, while, break, continue, and return. Choose conditionals for Boolean decisions, loops for repeated work, and matching for alternative data. Scope exits also run lexical cleanup.
Concept What you will learn Conditionals Branch on Bool values with if and else. Loops Iterate with for and while, and use break and continue. Pattern matching Handle alternatives exhaustively and bind their payloads.

title: Conditionals
content:
Conditionals# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index An if statement chooses whether to execute a block. An else block handles the other path.
fn status(active: Bool) -> String: if active: return "Active" else: return "Inactive"Conditions require Bool. The condition in this example is already a Boolean; numeric and text values do not acquire truth values implicitly.
if is a statement and does not produce a value. Evaluate its condition once; execute exactly one selected branch, or neither branch when the condition is false and no else is present. else aligns with the corresponding if. An additional conditional uses else if, not elif.
Each branch has its own lexical scope. Names declared in a branch are not visible after the conditional; assignments to an outer var affect that existing binding. An else if chain checks conditions in order and stops after selecting a branch.
fn classify(value: Int) -> String: if value < 0: return "negative" else if value == 0: return "zero" else: return "positive"if 1: is rejected because its condition is Int. let result = if active: ... is rejected because if is not an expression. Use branch-local assignment to a declared var or explicit returns to select a result. The function return rules determine whether all reachable paths return.
Validating inputs# Validation uses the same ordinary control flow as any other decision:
fn nonnegative(value: Int) -> Bool: if value < 0: return false return trueThe early return exits the function on the negative path. The final return runs on the remaining path. Expected failures uses this structure to reject invalid input with a domain error.
Bindings after a branch# Every binding is initialized at declaration. To select a value for use after the conditional, initialize an outer var and assign to it in the branches. Branch-local names stay inside their branch. See bindings .
Use pattern matching when the decision depends on which case of an alternative value is present.
Previous: Function values and closures · Next: Loops

title: Loops
content:
Loops# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use for / in to traverse values and while to repeat a block while a Boolean condition holds. break exits a loop; continue proceeds to its next iteration.
Loops are statements, not expressions. Manuscript has no labeled loops, loop-result values, integer-range syntax, or user-defined iteration protocol.
Traversing a list# fn sum(values: List[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return totalThe list contains shareable integers. Each iteration binds an element and updates the accumulator. Addition uses checked Int arithmetic, so overflow is a programming fault .
Iterable types and binding# Evaluate a for’s iterable expression once before entering the loop. The loop introduces one immutable identifier per iteration; it does not accept a binding pattern or a type annotation. The closed set of supported iterables is:
Iterable Iteration binding type Traversal order List[T] T Position order Set[T] T Insertion order Map[K, V] MapEntry[K, V] Key insertion order MapEntry[K, V] is an immutable record with fields key: K and value: V. It uses the map’s key/value eligibility requirements. Its type and named constructor MapEntry[K, V](key: key, value: value) are imported from @std/collections.ms; field access is ordinary record access. Iteration infers the entry type without requiring an import of its name. It is not a positional pair. Destructure an entry inside the body when convenient.
fn total(values: Map[String, Int]) -> Int: var sum = 0 for entry in values: let {key, value} = entry sum = sum + value return sumfor [key, value] in values: is rejected at parsing. Iterating a number, text, optional, function, or arbitrary object with a next method is rejected at type checking. Each iteration creates a new binding and lexical scope. Assigning to the iteration binding is rejected; an outer mutable accumulator can be reassigned.
Repeating while a condition holds# fn count_down(start: Int) -> Int: var remaining = start while remaining > 0: remaining = remaining - 1 return remainingThe condition is tested as a Bool. Each iteration updates remaining; the loop ends when the comparison is false.
A while reevaluates its condition before every iteration, including after continue. A for continues by selecting its next element and terminates after the last element. An empty iterable executes no body. A false initial while condition also executes no body.
Exiting an iteration# break and continue select the nearest enclosing loop within the same function body. They have no labels or arguments and are rejected outside a loop. An anonymous function inside a loop cannot break or continue that enclosing loop. return exits the current function, including when it appears in a loop body. Unreachable loop-control statements still need a valid enclosing loop.
break, continue, and return leave different control-flow paths, but each runs cleanup for the scopes it exits. Each loop iteration has its own scope. Resources registered with with in an iteration close when that iteration exits. A plain let declaration does not register cleanup. See lexical cleanup for the cleanup order and fault rules.
Cancellation# Each loop back-edge is a cancellation checkpoint, so CPU-bound loops respond promptly to cancellation without explicit calls. See propagation and checkpoints for all runtime checkpoints.
Previous: Conditionals · Next: Pattern matching

title: Pattern matching
content:
Pattern matching# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A match selects a block according to a value’s alternative. Each case can bind the data carried by that alternative.
A match accepts tagged alternative types, including Optional and Result. Matching numeric or Boolean literals, guards, ranges, nested case patterns, and combined patterns is rejected. match is a statement; it cannot initialize a binding as an expression. The scrutinee evaluates once.
The following function handles the Payment type declared in alternatives :
fn describe(payment: Payment) -> String: match payment: Paid(receipt): return "Paid: {receipt}" Declined(reason): return "Declined: {reason}" Pending(reference): return "Pending: {reference}"Payload patterns# Case payloads bind positions in the declaration’s field order. A pattern must give exactly one identifier or _ placeholder per payload field. Pattern payloads are positional even though constructors always use named fields. Nullary cases use a bare case name without ().
type Position: case Point(x: Int, y: Int) case Unknown fn horizontal(position: Position) -> Int: match position: Position.Point(horizontal_value, _): return horizontal_value Position.Unknown: return 0Point(x: local, y: other): is rejected at parsing. Point(x): is rejected for wrong arity. Repeated binding identifiers are rejected, while _ can occur repeatedly because it creates no name. Each arm’s payload bindings and body share a lexical scope nested inside the enclosing scope.
An unqualified case in a pattern resolves within the scrutinee’s alternative type. A qualified case must belong to that exact type. Other.Point(...) cannot match Position, even when its payload types have the same shape. Constructor-expression name lookup instead follows alternative construction .
Exhaustiveness# Match cases bind data without fallthrough; missing alternatives are compile errors. Wildcard cases must be explicit.
Every case in the example returns its own description. Running the Paid branch does not continue into Declined or Pending. The compiler checks that all alternatives are accounted for.
_: is the wildcard arm. It is permitted once, must be last, binds nothing, and covers every case not already handled. Duplicate cases, unknown cases, an arm after the wildcard, and a wildcard after all cases have been explicitly covered are rejected as invalid or unreachable arms. Qualified and unqualified spellings of the same case count as duplicates.
fn paid(payment: Payment) -> Bool: match payment: Paid(_): return true _: return falseAdding a case to an alternative invalidates exhaustive matches that lack a wildcard. A match with a wildcard remains exhaustive; its wildcard handles the new case. Return completeness is checked across all reachable arms using the function return rules .
Optional and result values# Optional and Result are also alternative types. Matching an optional distinguishes a present value from absence. Matching a result distinguishes success from an expected failure and lets the caller decide what to do with each.
Matching resource references# Matching binds ordinary payload values and references. No binding is consumed, and matching does not register resource cleanup. Destructuring bindings use brackets or braces; alternative match cases retain their Case(payload) syntax. See aggregate references .
Previous: Loops · Next: Expected failures with Result

title: Errors and validation
content:
Errors and validation# Core language guide · Design index Distinguish expected failures, missing values, and programming faults. Return Result for expected failures, use Optional for absence, and assert an invariant when its violation means the program is incorrect. Each has its own handling rules.
Concept What you will learn Expected failures with Result Return success or domain errors as ordinary values. Error propagation with try Forward compatible errors without hiding faults or cancellation. Assertions and programming faults Check invariants and understand task failure after cleanup.

title: Expected failures with Result
content:
Expected failures with Result# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Expected failures use Result, imported from @std/result.ms. Its map_error helper is a separate export from the same module. Runtime input validation uses ordinary control flow.
Result[T, E] has the alternatives ok(value: value) and error(cause: cause). Its type states both the success value and the expected failure. An error value is available to callers for handling through ordinary control flow.
Returning a domain error# type DiscountError: case InvalidPrice case InvalidPercent fn discount(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> Result[Decimal, DiscountError]: if price < 0d: return error(cause: InvalidPrice) if percent < 0d or percent > 100d: return error(cause: InvalidPercent) return ok(value: price * (1d - percent / 100d))The function checks inputs before calculating. It returns an explicit error for each invalid condition and wraps the calculated decimal in ok on success.
Handling the result# The following continues the declarations above:
fn discount_message(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> String: let outcome = discount(price: price, percent: percent) match outcome: ok(value): return "Discounted price: {value}" error(cause): return "Discount could not be calculated."This caller chooses a response for either outcome. Another caller could inspect cause with a further match or propagate it with try .
Results and concurrent execution# Returning error(cause: cause) is normal function completion. In parallel, the domain Result remains the operation’s return value and does not cancel siblings. The outer API result separately reports ExecutionError; see parallel operations . A Background service reports completion-only domain errors through its configured failure observer.
Use Optional for absence without an error explanation and assertions for programming invariants.
Previous: Pattern matching · Next: Error propagation with try

title: Error propagation with try
content:
Error propagation with try# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use try when a function should return an expected error from a called operation instead of handling it locally.
try expression unwraps ok; on error, it returns that error from the enclosing function. The function must return a compatible Result.
The following continues the discount and DiscountError declarations in expected failures :
fn discounted_label(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> Result[String, DiscountError]: let value = try discount(price: price, percent: percent) return ok(value: "Discounted price: {value}")Success and failure paths# When discount returns ok, value contains the Decimal payload and the function builds its label. When it returns error, the enclosing function returns that error instead of executing the remaining statements.
The success types differ: the called function returns a decimal, while the enclosing function returns text. Both use DiscountError, so the error can be forwarded unchanged.
Error compatibility# Error conversion uses the standard map_error(result: outcome, transform: fn(cause: E) -> F) adapter or an explicit match; its exact signature and single-evaluation rule are in the standard API contract . A caller with a different error contract must translate the error explicitly. try does not invent a conversion or combine unrelated error types into an implicit union.
Precisely, an operand Result[T, E] has success type T, and the enclosing function must return Result[U, E] with the same exact error type E. Its success type U may differ. Merely implementing a common contract does not make two error types compatible; explicit contract conversion must occur before building the operand result.
The operand evaluates once. Prefix try binds more tightly than arithmetic, so try operation() + 1 means (try operation()) + 1. An operand that is not a Result, a mismatched error type, or try inside a Unit function or Unit test body is rejected. For an anonymous function, the enclosing function is that anonymous function, not its caller or containing body. See expressions and type compatibility .
Cleanup and cancellation# try does not catch programming faults or parent cancellation. A propagated error is a return path and performs lexical cleanup for the scopes it leaves. A programming fault or parent cancellation follows its own unwinding rules.
Previous: Expected failures with Result · Next: Assertions and programming faults

title: Assertions and programming faults
content:
Assertions and programming faults# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A programming fault signals a broken invariant. Expected bad inputs should be validated with control flow and represented by Result when the caller needs a failure value.
Assertions# assert condition checks a programming invariant and produces a fault when false.
The condition must have type Bool and is evaluated once. assert is a statement, not a value-producing expression; numeric or text conditions are rejected.
fn discount_validated(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> Decimal: assert price > 0d assert percent > 0d assert percent < 100d return price * (1d - percent / 100d)This example expects strictly positive prices and percentages below 100 as preconditions. A violation is treated as a programming fault. Use the validating discount function in expected failures when these values come from ordinary runtime input.
Explicit faults# An explicit panic(message: message) produces a programming fault when code determines that an invariant has failed.
Its source type is fn(message: String) -> Never. It never completes normally; a call can appear where any expression result type is expected, including an Int return position. This does not create a catchable expected-error value or permit normal fallthrough in a non-Unit function. See Unit, Never, and return completeness .
panic(message: "Required invariant was violated.")A fault aborts the current operation after cleanup. Programming faults are distinct from expected Result errors.
Cleanup and observation# Cleanup still runs after a fault. A cleanup fault can replace a pending return, domain error, or cancellation, while secondary faults are retained as diagnostics. The full selection and cleanup rules are in lexical cleanup .
An active parallel caller observes an operation fault as ExecutionError.Crashed after siblings are cancelled and joined. Background faults go to the service’s failure observer. A caller’s own fault still unwinds it; try only propagates Result errors. See execution errors .
Previous: Error propagation with try

title: Standard library
content:
Standard library guide# Design index Choose standard types and runtime facilities by the lifetime, cancellation, and authority contracts they provide.
Reading order# 1. Standard types # Core and standard types Standard imports and API typing 2. Concurrent APIs and host lifetimes # Bounded parallel mapping Background services 3. Data, state, and I/O # Minimum data operations Readers, writers, and streams Bounded queues Synchronized state, pools, and leases Local builders and immutable snapshots 4. Application hosts # HTTP request hosts CLI application hosts Runtime facilities# These are ordinary library facilities with effect, sharing, lifetime, and cancellation contracts. They add no concurrency syntax. Host-created requests, sessions, applications, and CLI runs establish fixed execution contexts. Parallel APIs join before returning; background services implement Closeable and join during shutdown.
Standard imports, immutable data, CLI streams, and concurrent APIs have concrete signatures. Queue, pool, builder, HTTP, and subprocess APIs still need details. See outstanding decisions .

title: Standard types
content:
Standard types# Guide index · Design index The catalog identifies intrinsic and imported standard values; the core language guide explains their syntax.
Core and standard types Standard imports and API typing

title: Core and standard types
content:
Core and standard types# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Type Meaning Import from Bool true or false Implicit intrinsic Int Signed 64-bit integer; checked arithmetic Implicit intrinsic Float IEEE 754 binary64 Implicit intrinsic Decimal Base-10, 34 significant digits; round half to even @std/decimal.ms String Immutable, valid UTF-8 text Implicit intrinsic Bytes Immutable byte sequence @std/bytes.ms Unit One value, unit Implicit intrinsic Never No possible value Implicit intrinsic List[T], Map[K, V], Set[T] Immutable homogeneous collections with their declared sharing bounds @std/collections.ms MapEntry[K, V] Immutable standard record with key: K and value: V; map iteration yields entries @std/collections.ms Optional[T] some(value: value) or none @std/optional.ms Result[T, E] ok(value: value) or error(cause: cause) @std/result.ms ExecutionError Joined-group timeout or crash @std/tasks.ms Background Synchronized service managing work under a fixed lifetime @std/tasks.ms WorkStatus, StartError, BackgroundFailure Background status, admission failure, and failure reports @std/tasks.ms OperationId Identity of a runtime operation, used for diagnostics and Background status/cancellation @std/tasks.ms Closeable Standard close() -> Unit cleanup contract @std/cleanup.ms File, ReadStream, WriteStream Resource contracts; standard host values use shared views with synchronized lifecycle checks @std/io.ms Duration, Instant Checked nanosecond duration and monotonic clock instant @std/time.ms Process CLI authority roots @std/cli.ms Files, IoError File capability contract and expected I/O failures @std/io.ms Clock Monotonic clock capability contract @std/time.ms Functions and closures are ordinary values; runtime tasks are not exposed as source ownership types. Fixed parallel result packs preserve positional types and use bracket destructuring; they are not homogeneous lists.
References do not extend an object’s open lifetime. Use with for deterministic release and Result for expected operation failures. See parallel , background services , and Closeable .
The standard API contract defines visibility, signatures, optional arguments, and pack typing.

title: Standard imports and API typing
content:
Standard imports and API typing# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index This page defines standard exports and their binding rules. A trusted manifest may implement them, but cannot change their source identities or typing rules. The implicit prelude contains only the six intrinsic types and three compiler bounds; every declaration below is imported explicitly. Native implementation and compiler support do not make a name globally visible.
Names and identity# Every module implicitly sees only Bool, Int, Float, String, Unit, Never, Shareable, Equal, and Hashable, as specified by module declarations . The three bounds describe compiler-verified sharing, equality, and hashing; ordinary behavior requirements use imported operation contracts. Keep new facilities in the standard library rather than expanding this list.
@std is a reserved directory supplied by the pinned compiler/runtime distribution. Each path below is a standard module, and each name is an individual export. There are no wildcard imports or automatic imports of other exports from the same module.
Module Exports @std/decimal.ms Decimal @std/bytes.ms Bytes @std/collections.ms List, Map, Set, MapEntry @std/optional.ms Optional @std/result.ms Result, map_error @std/cleanup.ms Closeable @std/tasks.ms parallel, parallel_map, check_cancelled, ExecutionError, OperationId, Background, BackgroundFailure, WorkStatus, StartError @std/faults.ms panic @std/time.ms Duration, Instant, Clock @std/io.ms Files, File, ReadStream, WriteStream, IoError @std/cli.ms Process import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms"Imports establish stable nominal identities independent of the application. Imported names follow ordinary collision and shadowing rules; unimported standard names are not reserved. A local declaration with the same spelling never acquires standard operators, cleanup recognition, callback checks, or native members.
Syntax and compiler support# Some library identities need compiler support while remaining explicit exports:
Ordinary bracket literals require the canonical List import in the module. The tasks literal of the imported parallel binding is a positional pack and does not require List. A d-suffixed literal requires the canonical Decimal import. Decimal arithmetic and interpolation keep their specified behavior. Optional and Result are standard alternatives with ordinary case lookup. try recognizes the canonical Result identity; a user-defined alternative named Result does not qualify. for, collection derivation, and guarded layout recognize the standard collection identities. MapEntry is an exported record; map iteration can infer it without importing its name. with recognizes the canonical Closeable implementation, or an operation contract declaring the exact close signature. A module writing impl Closeable or a Closeable bound imports that name; using an already-typed resource does not require an otherwise unused import. Runtime API special checks attach to the resolved standard callee. A user-defined parallel is an ordinary function and never receives pack or callable-proof rules. A missing or substituted List/Decimal import rejects the corresponding literal during resolution/type checking. Inferred library values may be matched, traversed, or used through their declared members without importing every type in their public signatures. Naming such a type or using its unqualified expression constructors requires its own import. Primitive receiver members in the data API are fixed standard bindings and can likewise produce inferred library values; they add no ambient type names. Imports supply declarations, not files, clocks, or other external authority.
OperationId is the single opaque, shareable identity for runtime operations, whether started by a joined group or admitted by a Background service. It has no source constructor and no implicit equality or hashing, and it grants no scheduling, joining, or transfer authority. A Background service’s status and cancel act only on IDs it admitted. WorkStatus has nullary cases Running, Succeeded, Failed, Cancelled, Crashed, and Unknown; qualify these case names when necessary. StartError has Closed and Full. IoError has Closed, InvalidInput, Unavailable, and Failed(message: String). These are shareable alternatives. Execution errors are defined in joining .
fn panic(message: String) -> Never fn check_cancelled() -> Unit fn map_error[T, E, F](result: Result[T, E], transform: fn(cause: E) -> F) -> Result[T, F]These lines specify bindings rather than complete source modules. check_cancelled unwinds the current execution if it has stopped; it returns Unit otherwise. map_error returns an unchanged success payload, or invokes transform(cause: cause) exactly once for an error. It invokes no callback for success and does not catch faults or cancellation. It is sequential and imposes no additional sharing bound.
Joined concurrency# All concurrency names are explicit library exports. The calls below require the individual parallel or parallel_map import from @std/tasks.ms; no concurrency operation, error type, work identity, or service expands the intrinsic type/bound list. Every concurrency name, including check_cancelled and OperationId, is exported by @std/tasks.ms. Timeouts and scheduling are implemented by library/runtime bindings.
parallel requires tasks and permits only the optional named argument timeout: Duration. Omission means no added limit; an inherited deadline still applies. Negative timeouts fault. Zero-timeout, stop, join, and outcome rules follow joining outcomes .
tasks must be a bracket literal, optionally grouped in parentheses. Each position must independently resolve to a shareable zero-parameter function fn() -> Ri; each Ri must be shareable. The binding produces Result[Pack[R1, …, Rn], ExecutionError]. Here Pack is compiler notation, with no source type-name spelling or source constructor. Existing lists are rejected; dynamic homogeneous work uses parallel_map.
Standard concurrency callbacks require the argument’s callable sharing proof . Function types themselves do not satisfy Shareable; an operation cannot return another function as a shareable result. Task preparation retains callback proofs internally, while result-pack sharing follows each result type.
Direct calls only# parallel, parallel_map, the Background constructor, and Background.start may appear only as the resolved callee of a direct call. A plain function signature cannot retain their callback-proof requirements.
parallel_map[Int, Int](...) is allowed when its callback has the required proof. let mapper = parallel_map[Int, Int], let launch = background.start, and passing either binding to a helper are rejected. Other standard operations follow ordinary function-value rules. Sequential map_error may be specialized and stored as a value. Source contracts cannot express these callback-proof requirements. Restricted background submission views are therefore unsupported.
Inferred result packs# A pack can be inferred into a local, carried through an inferred generic type argument, bound in a Result match, returned through a generic T, and destructured with exact positional arity. It cannot be written in an annotation, explicit type argument, field, or named function signature. Nested inferred packs retain their exact shape. Pack identity is the ordered sequence of position types; the empty pack is distinct from Unit and List. Packs derive Shareable position by position, but have no equality, hashing, iteration, field access, or indexing. Generic helpers such as map_error can therefore preserve a parallel pack without a new source syntax.
fn parallel_map[T: Shareable, U: Shareable]( items: List[T], operation: fn(item: T) -> U, limit: Int, ) -> Result[List[U], ExecutionError]This binding additionally permits the same optional timeout argument. operation must be shareable and must use the exact parameter label item. The result is in input order. A nonpositive limit faults before any operation starts. This binding has no label polymorphism or overloaded source declaration.
Background service# Background(limit: Int) constructs a synchronized native service under the current execution context. limit must be positive. Its only optional arguments are reporter: fn(failure: BackgroundFailure) -> Unit, drain: Duration, and history_limit: Int. The defaults are the host diagnostic sink, zero drain, and 128 completed statuses. drain and history_limit must be nonnegative. A supplied reporter must be shareable; retained reporter captures must remain usable through service shutdown.
type BackgroundFailure: case Failed(operation: OperationId, cause: String) case Crashed(operation: OperationId, message: String) # Operations of the native Background service: fn start(operation: fn() -> Result[Unit, String]) -> Result[OperationId, StartError] fn cancel(id: OperationId) -> Unit fn status(id: OperationId) -> WorkStatus fn close() -> Unitstart requires a shareable callable. This is one operation signature: Operations without domain errors explicitly return ok(value: unit), and operations with domain error types explicitly translate them to String using map_error or match. There is no generic method, implicit formatting of arbitrary errors, or overload. Background explicitly implements Closeable in the standard binding.
Failure reporting# The reporter receives Failed for a returned String error and Crashed for a programming fault. Cancellation changes status rather than producing a domain error. Reporter calls are serialized, may suspend, and run outside transition locks under a shielded service context. Shutdown waits for them.
At most limit completion reports may be pending. Capacity exhaustion or a reporter fault sends both the original diagnostic and the reporting failure/overflow diagnostic to the host sink. A reporter fault never invokes the reporter recursively. The sink itself has a bounded buffer; overflow increments a retained counter and emits a host stderr diagnostic. Uncooperative reporters remain subject to host escalation.
Status eviction never reuses an ID for different work. An ID the service did not admit, including one from another service or a joined group, returns Unknown from status and is a no-op for cancellation.
Capabilities and data operations# The host’s authority roots and stream signatures are defined by CLI hosts and streams . Standard collection, byte, text, numeric, and duration members are defined in minimum data operations . Source code cannot add implementations or members to intrinsic or standard native types. Source types may implement standard contracts in their own defining module.
General user type packs, optional source parameters, generic operations, and third-party dependency package imports are unsupported. HTTP host registration still needs an API contract.
Data services and additional host capabilities# @std/queues.ms exports Queue and QueueError; @std/state.ms exports State; @std/pools.ms exports Pool, Lease, and PoolError; @std/builders.ms exports ListBuilder, MapBuilder, SetBuilder, BytesBuilder, and StringBuilder. Their exact contracts live in queues , state and pools , and builders . None is ambient. Opaque constructor parameter names are not source fields.
@std/time.ms also exports sleep(duration: Duration) -> Unit, a sequential cancellable delay. Negative duration faults; zero performs a cancellation checkpoint.
@std/http.ms exports the bounded request host types in HTTP . Network.serve is a direct-call-only operation requiring a proved shareable handler. @std/process.ms exports Commands, CommandOutput, and CommandError in streams . CLI Process additionally has network: Network & Shareable and commands: Commands & Shareable. Imports provide types, while those fields provide actual authority.

title: Concurrent APIs and host lifetimes
content:
Concurrency services# Guide index · Design index Choose joined operations for request work and explicit background services for work that outlives the caller. Every concurrency API and supporting type is an individual standard export; none enters the intrinsic prelude. See concurrency imports .
Parallel operations Bounded parallel mapping Background services

title: Bounded parallel mapping
content:
Bounded parallel mapping# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Import parallel_map from @std/tasks.ms. It runs the same function over a dynamic list, with a bounded number of active invocations. Its result is an ordinary homogeneous list in input order.
let lookup = fn(item: UserId) -> Result[User, UserError]: return users.get(id: item) let outcomes = try parallel_map( items: user_ids, operation: lookup, limit: 8, )The callable must use the exact parameter label item, as declared by the standard binding; each element is supplied as item: value. Other labels require an explicit wrapper and are rejected directly. Every invocation’s exact result is retained: this example returns List[Result[User, UserError]] inside the outer execution Result.
Naming Result or ExecutionError in a signature requires their individual imports from @std/result.ms and @std/tasks.ms. The inferred output list does not require a List import; a source bracket list literal does.
This body fragment requires an enclosing Result[U, ExecutionError] function for its outer try; translate with map_error when using an application error type. Unit tests must match the outer Result instead.
The captured users capability must retain a static shared contract type, such as Users & Shareable; a plain Users view cannot supply the callable’s sharing proof.
The callable’s captured environment, input elements, and output elements must satisfy the concurrent sharing bounds. Returning a resource reference does not register cleanup or keep it open; operations should manage temporary resources within their own with scopes.
limit must be positive. At most that many operations are active; pending elements remain in the bounded/input storage rather than creating an unbounded set of goroutines. Empty input produces an empty successful list. Domain errors are normal values and do not stop other invocations.
Stopping, joining, timeouts, and outcomes follow the shared joined-group contract ; stopping also prevents further items from starting.
This API replaces dynamic source task collections. No application owns, adopts, or retrieves individual task handles. Completion-order streaming is unsupported by this API. Bounded pipelines use the separate queue and background-service contracts.

title: Background services
content:
Background services# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Import Background from @std/tasks.ms. It starts and tracks operations under a fixed application or component lifetime. It implements Closeable; its callable requirements are defined by the standard API contract . Multiple instances can be constructed and passed through ordinary parameters.
with emails = Background(limit: 32): with indexing = Background(limit: 4): serve(emails: emails, indexing: indexing)The constructing host supplies the execution parent. Construct application services under the application lifetime, session services under the session lifetime, and request services under the request lifetime. Calling a service from another context never reparents it.
Starting work# import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" import Background from "@std/tasks.ms" import StartError from "@std/tasks.ms" import OperationId from "@std/tasks.ms" type MailError: case Rejected interface Mailer: fn send(to: String) -> Result[Unit, MailError] fn enqueue(emails: Background, mailer: Mailer & Shareable, address: String) -> Result[OperationId, StartError]: let send = fn() -> Result[Unit, String]: return map_error( result: mailer.send(to: address), transform: fn(cause: MailError) -> String: return "Email delivery failed" ) return emails.start(operation: send)Admission is nonblocking and atomic with closure and capacity reservation. limit bounds admitted operations that have not yet committed their completion; accepted work starts without an additional unbounded queue. A slot is freed when completion commits, before failure reporting, so a slow reporter does not throttle admission. Rejected work never runs. Automatic retries are not part of start.
Background operations return Result[Unit, String]: explicit ok(value: unit) on success, or a String error after domain-error adaptation. Successful operations produce status; failures reach the reporter. One operation’s failure does not cancel unrelated operations.
The returned OperationId is the same identity used in execution errors, failure reports, and traces. With this service, it supports status and cancellation without transferring shutdown responsibility. The standard API contract defines signatures, status retention, constructor defaults, bounded reporting, and fallback diagnostics.
Closures retain ordinary captured references. Capture a request-data snapshot and application services, then acquire resources inside the operation’s own with blocks. Capturing a request’s resource does not extend its lifetime; use after close returns a resource-specific error. Closure syntax is the ordinary syntax in function values and closures .
Bind the operation’s data in an ordinary closure; there is no function-plus-arguments submission form.
Lifetime and shutdown# Pass Background directly. Its start binding follows the direct-call restriction . Sharing or dropping a service reference or work ID does not change its lifetime or cancel work. Work never transfers between services.
close() -> Unit is idempotent and does not finish until admitted work and its cleanup have ended:
Close admission atomically across all aliases. Allow a configured drain period; the default is no drain delay. Request cancellation of unfinished operations. Join every admitted operation and finish bounded reporting/cleanup. Cancelling a submitting request does not cancel accepted work. Cancelling the service’s fixed parent does cancel its operations, even if a drain period was configured. A service’s close cannot join itself; host/component code outside its operations performs shutdown.
Hosts choose overall budgets, admission/reporting settings, and an escalation policy for uncooperative work. Expiry is not successful joining; the runtime cannot forcibly terminate an arbitrary goroutine safely. Closing a service before closing its application dependencies is required.
This is process-local execution, not durable delivery. Work that must survive restart needs a durable queue. If acknowledgement can be lost during request cancellation, use application idempotency keys to make resubmission safe.
Runtime and library responsibilities# The Go runtime supplies operation start, stop, join, and synchronization. Admission, reporting, and shutdown policy can be implemented over those primitives. The initial implementation may provide the service in Go behind the same imported API. These native primitives are implementation details, not source intrinsics. The compiler validates the standard binding’s callable proofs; service admission, status retention, reporting, drain, cancellation, and joining remain library/runtime behavior.

title: Data, state, and I/O
content:
Data, state, and I/O# Guide index · Design index These facilities support bounded communication, scoped resources, and local construction.
Minimum data operations Readers, writers, and streams Bounded queues Synchronized state, pools, and leases Local builders and immutable results

title: Minimum data operations
content:
Minimum data operations# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index These standard native members form the data API. Their signatures belong to the canonical intrinsic or imported standard receiver type; they do not expand the intrinsic name or bound list. Import standard types when naming them, including List for ordinary bracket literals. Inferred return types and receiver members do not require importing otherwise unused type names. They use ordinary named calls with the exact labels below. Updates return new immutable values and leave every alias of the original unchanged. Allocation failure is a host failure. Sizes and indexes use Int.
Collections# Receiver or constructor Signature/result List[T] length() -> Int; get(index: Int) -> Optional[T] List[T] append(value: T) -> List[T]; concat(values: List[T]) -> List[T] Map[K, V]() Empty Map[K, V] Map[K, V] length() -> Int; get(key: K) -> Optional[V]; contains(key: K) -> Bool Map[K, V] with_entry(key: K, value: V) -> Map[K, V]; without(key: K) -> Map[K, V] Set[T]() Empty Set[T] Set[T] length() -> Int; contains(value: T) -> Bool Set[T] with_value(value: T) -> Set[T]; without(value: T) -> Set[T] All existing element and key bounds apply. An empty Map/Set constructor requires explicit type arguments or a complete expected application; it supplies no inference evidence by itself. List construction uses the existing bracket literal. Negative or out-of-range list indexes return none. A size exceeding MaxInt64 faults.
Maps and sets traverse in insertion order. Replacing an equal map key retains its original key value and first insertion position; adding an existing set element retains its original value and position. Removing an absent key/element is a value-preserving operation. Removing and then adding places the new entry at the end. Equality remains independent of insertion order. A simple implementation may copy storage on update; builder APIs are specified separately once their signatures are settled.
import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Map from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" fn positives(values: List[Int]) -> List[Int]: var result: List[Int] = [] for value in values: if value > 0: result = result.append(value: value) return result test "dynamic immutable data": assert positives(values: [3, -1, 2]) == [3, 2] let absent: Optional[Int] = none assert [1].get(index: 5) == absent let original = Map[String, Int]().with_entry(key: "a", value: 1) let updated = original.with_entry(key: "b", value: 2).with_entry(key: "a", value: 3) assert original.get(key: "a") == some(value: 1) assert updated.get(key: "a") == some(value: 3)Strings and bytes# Receiver or constructor Signature/result String byte_length() -> Int; to_bytes() -> Bytes; parse_int() -> Optional[Int] Bytes(values: List[Int]) Immutable bytes; each value must be 0–255, otherwise a programming fault Bytes length() -> Int; get(index: Int) -> Optional[Int]; concat(values: Bytes) -> Bytes Bytes to_text() -> Optional[String] String.to_bytes uses UTF-8. Bytes.to_text succeeds exactly for valid UTF-8, preserving contents without normalization; invalid bytes produce none. Byte get follows list index behavior and returns the unsigned byte as Int. An empty Bytes(values: []) is valid.
parse_int accepts exactly an optional ASCII + or - followed by one or more ASCII decimal digits and an in-range mathematical value. It permits leading zeros, rejects whitespace, separators, fractions, exponents, and any unconsumed character, and returns none for invalid or out-of-range input. Runtime parsing is distinct from the stricter source literal grammar. Scalar/grapheme indexing and additional parsing/formatting APIs are unsupported.
import Bytes from "@std/bytes.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" test "explicit byte conversion": assert "é".byte_length() == 2 assert "é".to_bytes().to_text() == some(value: "é") let invalid: Optional[String] = none assert Bytes(values: [255]).to_text() == invalid assert "-007".parse_int() == some(value: -7)Numeric and time conversion# Receiver Signature/result Int to_float() -> Float; to_decimal() -> Decimal Float truncate_to_int() -> Optional[Int] Decimal to_float() -> Float; truncate_to_int() -> Optional[Int] Int milliseconds, seconds, minutes members producing Duration Int→Decimal is exact. Int→Float and Decimal→Float round once to nearest binary64, ties to even. Decimal→Float may produce signed infinity or signed zero under the Float rules. Truncation discards the fractional part toward zero, then checks the mathematical integer against the exact signed 64-bit limits before conversion. NaN, infinities, or an out-of-range integer yield none; do not compare against a rounded Float representation of MaxInt64 and then use a Go cast.
Duration is a signed 64-bit count of nanoseconds. The three unit members work on any Int expression and multiply by 1,000,000, 1,000,000,000, or 60,000,000,000 with overflow checks. Instant is an opaque monotonic instant in the current run’s clock domain; it has no source constructor. Clock adapters and injected test clocks must preserve a single comparable domain within a run. Cross-domain comparison or subtraction faults. Duration arithmetic and Instant shifts/differences check overflow; these compiler-defined operations are enumerated in the operator table .
Boundary expectations: 1e300.truncate_to_int() is none; converting Float +2^63 to Int is none, while Float -2^63 succeeds. 2.seconds is 2,000,000,000 nanoseconds. Unsupported unit names and mixed arithmetic such as 2.seconds + 1 are type errors.

title: Readers, writers, and streams
content:
Readers, writers, and streams# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The stream contracts have explicit cleanup operations and admit both native implementations and source fakes. The standard host exposes ReadStream & Shareable, WriteStream & Shareable, and File & Shareable views of its synchronized receivers. Bare stream contract types remain plain views under the ordinary interface rules.
interface ReadStream: fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn close() -> Unit interface WriteStream: fn write(data: Bytes) -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn close() -> Unit interface File: fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn close() -> UnitRead requires positive max_bytes or returns IoError.InvalidInput. ok(some(bytes)) contains 1 through max_bytes bytes; ok(none) is EOF. Empty chunks never represent EOF. The bound limits each read, not total file size. Write waits until all bytes are accepted or an error occurs; empty writes succeed without I/O. An error may follow a partial external write and supplies no rollback. Internal buffering is bounded with backpressure.
Native wrappers serialize simultaneous reads/writes without holding a lifecycle lock during blocking I/O. Close marks admission closed, interrupts active I/O where supported, waits for admitted I/O to end, and releases the handle once. Later calls return IoError.Closed. Concurrent close callers wait for the same release/fault. A flag check followed by unsynchronized handle use is insufficient. Uncancellable I/O can delay release and requires host escalation; expected completion errors belong to read/write, and unexpected release failures are cleanup faults.
Plain and shared contract values declaring these exact close operations are eligible for with under Closeable ; cleanup does not require concurrent sharing. Source fakes implement the selected stream contract and explicitly construct shared views when substituting for standard host roots or acquisitions; no native File constructor or contract inheritance is needed. Adapters honor cancellation and undelivered acquisition . The bounded subprocess facility is exported by @std/process.ms. The CLI host supplies process.commands: Commands & Shareable:
# Commands fn run(program: String, arguments: List[String], input: Bytes, max_output_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[CommandOutput, CommandError] type CommandOutput: exit_code: Int stdout: Bytes stderr: BytesCommandError has InvalidInput, Unavailable, TimedOut, OutputLimit, and Failed(message: String). Empty/NUL program names, NUL arguments, negative bounds, and negative timeout return InvalidInput. The total stdout plus stderr bound is nonnegative. Nonzero ordinary exit is an ok output with that code. Timeout or output overflow stops and joins the process before returning its error; caller cancellation unwinds after joining. POSIX process groups include descendants in termination. On platforms without process-group support the wrapper controls the direct process, with bounded pipe completion; descendant supervision needs a platform host contract. Interactive subprocess streams and network streaming remain separate future contracts.

title: Bounded queues
content:
Bounded queues# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A queue connects producers and consumers through synchronized, bounded storage. It carries shareable values.
Facility Contract Queue[T] Shareable elements; synchronized bounded queue; cancellable send/receive; explicit close Using the contract# Sending and receiving must respond to cancellation. Explicit close is part of the contract, so shutdown needs a deliberate end to admission and communication. A queue is a library facility and does not introduce another concurrency syntax.
API# Queue[T: Shareable](capacity: Int) creates synchronized storage with positive capacity. The queue is opaque, shareable, and neither equal nor hashable. A nonpositive capacity is a programming fault.
fn send(value: T) -> Result[Unit, QueueError] fn receive() -> Optional[T] fn close() -> UnitImport Queue and QueueError from @std/queues.ms; QueueError has the nullary case Closed. Send waits for space, receive waits for a value, and both respond to caller cancellation. Close atomically stops send admission and wakes all waiters. Already buffered values drain in FIFO order; once drained, receive returns none, including repeated receives. Blocked and later senders return error(cause: QueueError.Closed). Close is idempotent and is eligible for with. A committed send or receive may precede cancellation; cancellation does not roll back queue effects.
See shareable collection elements and cooperative cancellation .

title: Synchronized state, pools, and leases
content:
Synchronized state, pools, and leases# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Shared application state and pools are synchronized services. A pool lease is an ordinary resource object registered with with and returned to the pool by close().
Pool references can be shared by requests and background work. A job acquires its own lease under its own scope. Retaining a lease reference does not prolong its lease lifetime.
Access and closure must be coordinated: close waits for or cancels outstanding operations before allowing reuse, and stale aliases report closed state rather than using a connection assigned to another caller. Supported simultaneous use is explicit in the adapter/service contract.
State# Import State from @std/state.ms. State[T: Shareable](value: T) is an opaque synchronized reference. get() -> T, set(value: T) -> Unit, and swap(value: T) -> T each execute atomically. Swap returns the previous value. A read followed by a write is not an atomic update. State is shareable but has no equality, hashing, or cleanup operation. Each operation checks caller cancellation before and after its transition; committed changes are not rolled back.
Pools and leases# Import Pool, Lease, and PoolError from @std/pools.ms. Pool[T](resources: List[T]) owns a nonempty fixed collection of distinct resource receivers. T must be a concrete shared operation-contract view declaring close() -> Unit. Construct views explicitly before pooling; a type variable’s implementation bound does not establish this representation at construction. The supplied resources must remain under the pool’s exclusive lifecycle management.
# Pool[T] fn acquire() -> Result[Lease[T], PoolError] fn close() -> Unit # Lease[T] fn get() -> Result[T, PoolError] fn close() -> UnitAcquire waits cancellably for capacity. Closed admission returns PoolError.Closed. Delivery that loses to cancellation releases its lease before unwind. Pool and lease objects are shareable, opaque, and eligible for with; they have no equality or hashing.
Get returns a guarded contract view. Calls through that view admit under the lease’s lifetime, including method values saved before release. Closing the view releases the lease. Lease close stops admission, cancels and joins admitted operations, and returns capacity exactly once; concurrent closers join the same release. A later get returns Closed. Stale I/O views return IoError.Closed; stale operations without an I/O error result fault. Release during an admitted operation interrupts it; I/O reports Closed, and other contracts report a programming fault unless caller cancellation already applies.
Pool close stops acquisition, wakes waiters, invalidates every lease, joins its operations, then closes owned receivers in reverse supplied order. It is idempotent; concurrent callers observe the same release fault. A lease or pool cannot join its own active operation. Closing may wait indefinitely for uncooperative native code; shutdown escalation is separate.
See sharing , release , and background resources .

title: Local builders and immutable results
content:
Local builders and immutable results# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A builder supports mutable local construction and creates an immutable snapshot when frozen. Builder aliases are ordinary references; freezing may seal the builder so later mutation reports a runtime error.
Builders with unsynchronized mutable state are not eligible for concurrent sharing. There is no consuming function type or compiler-tracked ownership transfer. Frozen contents follow the ordinary collection element bounds.
API# All builder names are exported by @std/builders.ms. They have zero-argument constructors and are opaque local references with no sharing, equality, or hashing eligibility. Type arguments can come from an explicit application or a complete expected constructor type.
Type Mutation Freeze result ListBuilder[T: Shareable] append(value: T) -> Unit List[T] MapBuilder[K: Hashable, V: Shareable] with_entry(key: K, value: V) -> Unit Map[K, V] SetBuilder[T: Hashable] with_value(value: T) -> Unit Set[T] BytesBuilder append(value: Int) -> Unit, concat(values: Bytes) -> Unit Bytes StringBuilder append(value: String) -> Unit String freeze() seals the shared local object and returns its immutable snapshot. Repeated freeze returns the same value. Every mutation through any alias after sealing is a programming fault. Byte append requires 0 through 255. Map replacement preserves insertion position; set insertion ignores an already present value. Builders have no implicit cleanup or ownership transfer.
See aggregates and collections .
