content:
Application hosts# Guide index · Design index Hosts establish fixed execution contexts and cancellation while enforcing application limits.
HTTP request hosts CLI application hosts

title: HTTP request hosts
content:
HTTP request hosts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index An HTTP host establishes a fixed execution context for each request, with admission limits, body limits, deadline policy, disconnect cancellation, backpressure, and fault isolation.
Request handlers use parallel or parallel_map for joined work and with for request resources. Client disconnection cancels the request and its nested groups; those groups join and registered cleanup runs before request execution ends.
Streaming responses remain within their request lifetime until streaming finishes. WebSocket/session hosts establish explicit session lifetimes and participate in shutdown; they are not untracked background goroutines.
Application background services are constructed under the application context and passed to handlers. Accepted work uses that service’s context, not the submitting request’s deadline or disconnect signal. Jobs capture request data and application services and acquire their own resources. Admission can race with request cancellation; idempotent submissions are an application concern.
Server shutdown stops request admission, allows a configured grace period, cancels and joins remaining request/session work, closes background admission and drains/cancels/joins those services, then releases application resources. A finite grace period does not guarantee uncooperative work exits; host escalation is separate.
Bounded request API# @std/http.ms exports Network, HttpServer, HttpRequest, and HttpResponse. The CLI host supplies process.network: Network & Shareable; source cannot manufacture native network authority.
type HttpRequest: method: String path: String query: String headers: Map[String, Bytes] body: Bytes type HttpResponse: status: Int headers: Map[String, String] body: Bytes # Network fn serve(address: String, handler: fn(request: HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse, limit: Int, max_body_bytes: Int, max_response_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration, grace: Duration) -> Result[HttpServer & Shareable, IoError] fn close() -> Unit # HttpServer fn address() -> String fn wait() -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn close() -> UnitThese signatures specify library operations. A complete declaration places the entire function header inside delimiter continuation. serve requires a direct call and a proved shareable handler; its plain method signature cannot preserve that requirement as a stored value. limit and timeout are positive; byte bounds and grace are nonnegative. Invalid settings return IoError.InvalidInput; binding failure returns Unavailable; a closed network returns Closed. Port zero permits an OS-selected port reported by address().
The host admits at most limit requests; excess requests receive 503 without invoking a handler. Bodies over the bound receive 413. Each handler gets a fixed timeout/disconnect context, and all work and cleanup in it join before its lifetime ends. Handler faults are isolated as 500 and recorded by the bounded diagnostic sink. Timeout/cancellation yields 504 where the connection still permits a response. Source routes by ordinary branching on method/path; raw query remains encoded. Header values are bytes to preserve non-UTF-8 HTTP input. Header keys are visited in sorted order.
Responses require status 200 through 599, a bounded body, and valid header names/values. Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, and Connection are host-managed and cannot be supplied. Invalid responses yield 500. This API is deliberately a bounded, fully buffered request/response host. Streaming, WebSocket/session registration, and HTTP client APIs are separate future contracts.
Server close stops admission, waits up to grace, then cancels and joins remaining requests and closes transport. It cannot be called from its own request. Network close joins all its servers. A server also registers with its construction execution lifetime, so omitting a with binding cannot detach server work. Unexpected transport release errors are cleanup faults; uncooperative handlers may delay joining beyond grace.
See background services , cancellation , and conformance programs .

title: CLI application hosts
content:
CLI application hosts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The CLI host has a fixed entry contract. The selected entry module must export exactly one nongeneric fn main(process: Process) -> Int; other exports are permitted. Missing/internal main or any different label/type/result is a compile error. The host creates one run context, constructs Process, invokes main once, and waits for work and cleanup before reporting exit.
Explicit authority roots# Process is a standard immutable record:
type Process: arguments: List[String] environment: Map[String, String] stdin: ReadStream & Shareable stdout: WriteStream & Shareable stderr: WriteStream & Shareable files: Files & Shareable clock: Clock & Shareable network: Network & Shareable commands: Commands & Shareable interface Clock: fn now() -> Instant interface Files: fn open(path: String) -> Result[File & Shareable, IoError]Arguments exclude the executable name. Environment is a snapshot; duplicate OS names are resolved by the host before entry. Invalid UTF-8 in process inputs is a startup failure on native stderr with exit 70 before main runs. Relative file paths use the fixed startup working directory. The specified file API opens read-only files; file creation remains an additional API contract. Network and command operations are specified in HTTP and subprocess execution .
The host creates Files, Clock, and stdio behind shared views. Those field types make Process shareable; Files.open preserves sharing in its returned File view. Applications and source fakes follow the same view-conversion rules .
Importing an interface supplies no authority. Files, clock, stdio, and environment arrive only through Process. The host closes roots after main and its scoped services finish; the application registers acquired files with with. Early root-stream closure affects every alias.
import Process from "@std/cli.ms" export fn main(process: Process) -> Int: let message = "Arguments: {process.arguments.length()}\n" match process.stdout.write(data: message.to_bytes()): ok(_): return 0 error(_): return 1This is a complete entry module. Only the Process type name is imported; field/method results and match cases are inferred from its public signatures. The import supplies the interface, while the host supplies the authority-bearing value. On success its transcript is Arguments: N followed by LF and exit 0. Stream signatures are defined in streams .
Exit and shutdown# Normal main results must be 0–125; other results fault. An unhandled root or cleanup fault exits 70 after attempted cleanup and reports primary/secondary diagnostics on host stderr. SIGINT/SIGTERM request cancellation; after joining and cleanup SIGINT exits 130 and SIGTERM exits 143. The first accepted stop reason is retained; a fault during joining/cleanup takes precedence and exits 70. Parent cancellation unwinds main rather than becoming a normal Result.
The ms run launcher forwards SIGINT/SIGTERM to the native host and waits for its joined shutdown before reporting that exit status.
Construct application Background services in main with with, inside their dependencies’ scopes. Shutdown stops admission, joins services, then releases roots. Uncooperative work/reporters can require host escalation ; the host exposes its watchdog policy. Escalated exit is incomplete cleanup, not conformance success.
Additional explicit roots# Process also exposes network: Network & Shareable and commands: Commands & Shareable for the bounded HTTP host and bounded subprocess execution . These capabilities are synchronized host roots. Network services register under their construction execution and join before host roots are released. The host provides no ambient networking or process constructor.

title: Resource lifetimes and cleanup
content:
Resource lifetimes and cleanup# Design index Ordinary values and object references use Go garbage collection. Explicit with scopes release external resources through the Closeable contract. Capturing, returning, storing, or passing a reference does not transfer cleanup or keep a resource open.
There is no move operation, borrowed parameter kind, or consuming closure type.
Reading order# 1. References and sharing# Ordinary references Concurrent access and resource lifetime Aggregates and local construction Assignment and branches 2. Scoped cleanup# With scopes The Closeable contract Scope-exit ordering Shielding and cleanup faults External resource release

title: References and sharing
content:
References and sharing# Guide index · Design index References determine access to objects. with registration determines cleanup. Concurrency safety and how long a resource stays open are separate properties.
Ordinary references Concurrent access and resource lifetime Aggregates and local construction Assignment and branches

title: Ordinary references
content:
Ordinary references# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Values are ordinary data or references to runtime objects. Passing, returning, storing, and capturing a reference keeps the same object accessible. It does not invalidate the previous binding, schedule cleanup, or extend a resource’s open lifetime.
Memory is reclaimed by Go garbage collection. External resources are released by explicit calls or with. Dropping an object reference, closure, or work ID is not an external cleanup operation.
A resource factory can return an open object for a caller to place in with. Returning an object already registered in a local with scope does not cancel that scope’s cleanup; callers receive a closed object after the function exits. Closed-resource access is a runtime error.
The design does not prevent every missed with registration at compile time. Libraries should expose scoped resource APIs and diagnostics for common omissions. There is no move or ownership-transfer mechanism.
See Closeable and closures .

title: Concurrent access and resource lifetime
content:
Concurrent access and resource lifetime# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Shareable means safe concurrent access. It does not keep a resource open or register cleanup. A closure may retain a resource after its with scope exits; later operations then report the resource’s closed-state error.
Data and services# Immutable data derives sharing from its components. Trusted native services declare sharing only when their mutable state and resource lifecycle are synchronized. A resource may serialize simultaneous calls or reject overlapping use explicitly.
Wrappers coordinate the closed-state check, access to the underlying handle, and closure as one lifecycle protocol. A flag check followed by unprotected I/O is insufficient. A stale lease must never access a connection reused for another caller.
Contract views# A plain contract view carries no sharing guarantee. Contract & Shareable retains a statically proved safe receiver through fields, parameters, returns, and collections. Explicit conversion to a plain view discards that proof; inspecting the hidden receiver cannot recover it. Contract views define construction and conversion.
A generic behavioral bound alone does not prove sharing; concurrent code needs T: Shareable & Contract. A shared receiver does not make its operation’s parameters or results shareable.
Function values# Function signatures describe calls, not captures. Source function types never satisfy the type-level Shareable bound. The compiler instead tracks a separate proof for each named function, closure, or bound method.
Boundary Callable sharing proof Named source function Safe: no captured local environment Local closure Safe when every capture has a type-level sharing guarantee or a retained callable proof Bound method Requires a shareable receiver; a plain view cannot reveal its hidden receiver’s proof Local copy or capture Retains the known proof var assignment or branch merge Requires the proof for every possible value Source function parameter or result, function field, or generic forwarding Erases the proof; concurrent invocation is rejected Direct standard callback argument Checks the value’s retained proof rather than a generic type bound A safe local closure therefore cannot instantiate F: Shareable. Passing it through identity[T] also loses its callable proof. These rules prevent storage or generic helpers from bypassing concurrent-call checks while preserving ordinary sequential function calls.
Capture application services and job data for background work, and acquire job resources inside that work’s own with scopes. See background services , generic bounds , and resource release .

title: Aggregates and local construction
content:
Aggregates and local construction# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Records, alternatives, collections, and closures can retain references to resource objects. An enclosing value does not become an owner or acquire an implicit destructor. Destructuring and matching bind ordinary data and references.
Closing a registered resource affects all aliases, including aliases nested in aggregates. Dropping an aggregate does not recursively close its fields. A library object that deliberately manages several resources can implement Closeable and explicitly close them in its implementation.
Collections retain their ordinary element bounds; resource references are eligible when their runtime wrappers satisfy the declared sharing contract. The bound provides concurrency safety, not a resource lifetime guarantee.
Builders follow the same reference rules; their API is still incomplete. Destructuring extracts fields and positions without changing cleanup.

title: Assignment and branches
content:
Assignment and branches# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index let prevents reassignment; var permits replacing a binding. Assignment changes a value or reference. It does not close the previous object or invalidate its aliases.
A with binding is immutable and registers the initialized object itself. Reassigning another variable that references the object cannot change which object’s close() will execute. Closing early is permitted because close() is idempotent.
Every binding is initialized at declaration. Branch-local names stay inside their branch; assignments to an outer var keep its declared type. Closures snapshot the current value of a local binding at creation; they do not share mutable local cells.
See bindings , closure captures , and with scopes .

title: Scoped cleanup
content:
Scoped cleanup# Guide index · Design index Use with to register a resource’s close() operation. Cleanup runs on every exit from that scope and remains separate from successful completion of the resource’s work.
With scopes The Closeable contract Scope-exit ordering Shielding and cleanup faults External resource release

title: With scopes
content:
With scopes# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index with initializes an immutable binding and registers the cleanup operation for exit from the indented body. A concrete type must explicitly implement Closeable; a contract type must explicitly declare fn close() -> Unit; a generic parameter must have a bound proving either operation, as specified by Closeable .
with file = try files.open(path: "data.txt"): let chunk = try file.read(max_bytes: 4096)This is a body fragment in a function returning Result[U, IoError], with an explicit files capability. A read returns Optional[Bytes]: match the chunk to distinguish data from EOF. The standard Files.open result retains a shared File view.
The initializer evaluates once. If it fails, no close action is registered. After successful acquisition, registration occurs before any further cancellation checkpoint. Fallthrough, break, continue, return, propagated error, programming fault, and cancellation execute the registered action for each scope exited, from inner to outer.
Resources acquired through with in a loop close at the end of that iteration. An ordinary resource-valued let declaration does not implicitly register cleanup. Returning or capturing a registered object does not remove the action.
with is the language construct; file, transaction, and Background behavior comes from ordinary contract implementations. There is no user-defined enter hook or error-suppression hook in this contract.
Go’s function-level defer does not have Manuscript’s block lifetime. The compiler explicitly lowers cleanup scopes and unwind paths. Go defer specification See Closeable , exit ordering , and lowering .

title: The Closeable contract
content:
The Closeable contract# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Import Closeable from @std/cleanup.ms when naming or implementing the standard cleanup contract. with checks its canonical identity rather than reserving its spelling. The standard declaration is:
interface Closeable: fn close() -> UnitFor a concrete value the compiler requires its explicit Closeable implementation, resolves that method, and registers a call to it. A contract value is also eligible when its own declaration explicitly contains the exact operation fn close() -> Unit; register that declared operation without a contract-to-contract conversion. A similarly named concrete method without impl Closeable remains insufficient. This rule lets standard File, ReadStream, and WriteStream contracts expose cleanup and admit source test fakes without inheritance. It has no special knowledge of a particular file or transaction. Libraries can implement the same cleanup contract for their own managed objects.
A generic parameter with a Closeable bound also supplies the implementation proof needed by with; dispatch its bound close operation directly without constructing a view or adding Shareable. A generic bound naming a contract that explicitly declares the exact close signature is likewise sufficient. An unconstrained type parameter or a merely similarly named method is insufficient.
close() is idempotent, may suspend like any other function, and finishes the object’s release/shutdown obligation before returning. Repeated or concurrent calls do not release an underlying handle twice. An implementation must coordinate ongoing access with closure and ensure that later accesses report closed state.
Expected failures that application code needs to handle belong to explicit operations such as commit(), flush(), or finish(), returning Result. The automatic close hook returns Unit; an unexpected release failure is a programming/cleanup fault, not a discarded error value.
A close failure does not skip other registered actions. Implementations must leave the object unusable or safely quarantined after a failed release rather than exposing an invalid/reused native handle. Faults and remaining release obligations are reported to the host.
General user defer syntax is unsupported. Custom scope cleanup can be packaged in a library object implementing Closeable.
See with scopes , cleanup faults , and operation contracts .

title: Scope-exit ordering
content:
Scope-exit ordering# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A scope’s registered with cleanup executes on every exit path. Ordinary aliases and aggregates do not add automatic release actions.
Evaluate the pending return value or select the initiating error, fault, or cancellation. Finish any active joined API call: it cancels unfinished operations if needed and joins them before unwinding into the caller’s cleanup. Call registered close() methods in reverse registration/nesting order. A Background.close() performs its own service cancellation and joining here. Deliver the pending return/error, unless cleanup selected a programming fault; otherwise propagate the selected fault or cancellation. A cleanup fault suppresses a pending normal return or domain error. The unreturned value is released for garbage collection; it is not recursively closed. Resource factories retain explicit responsibility for resources acquired but never delivered.
Returned references do not bypass registered cleanup. A returned file registered in the exiting scope is already closed when the caller receives it. There is no staged ownership transfer or result escrow.
Register dependencies outside the background service’s with scope so that service shutdown finishes before those dependencies close. See background services and fault selection .

title: Shielding and cleanup faults
content:
Shielding and cleanup faults# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Cleanup runs even when the initiating execution was cancelled or faulted. It ignores the initiating cancellation and expired work deadline while retaining the original capability authority. It may suspend.
Each registered action is attempted once by its scope exit. A fault in one action does not skip remaining actions. The first programming fault is primary; later cleanup faults are attached as secondary diagnostics. If no programming fault was already pending, a cleanup fault replaces a normal return, domain error, or cancellation. Without a cleanup fault, the initiating outcome is preserved.
At a concurrency API boundary a programming fault produces Crashed in the outer ExecutionError. At a background boundary it is reported by the service. Root hosts isolate and report request failures.
Hosts configure cleanup watchdogs and escalation independently of request timeouts. Shielding does not guarantee that uncooperative code terminates, and a timer cannot make a still-running close/join count as completed. The runtime may require process-level escalation.
Expected failures are handled through explicit fallible completion methods before scope exit. See Closeable , timeouts , and resource release .

title: External resource release
content:
External resource release# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Files, sockets, stream bodies, transactions, and pool leases are ordinary runtime objects implementing Closeable. Their memory is garbage collected; release of external handles or activity is explicit or scoped with with.
Object Automatic close behavior File, socket, stream body Release the external handle Transaction Roll back if not committed; then release its lease Connection lease Return the connection only after outstanding access has ended Background service Stop admission, cancel as configured, and join work Closing is shared state: all aliases see the same closed object. Resource methods return resource-specific errors such as IoError.Closed after closure. The wrapper must synchronize access and close; checking a flag before accessing a native handle is not sufficient. Old lease references must never access a connection reused for another caller.
Cleanup is not successful completion. Explicit commit, finish, or flush operations expose expected errors with Result. Unexpected release failures become cleanup faults. A plain let, function call, aggregate, or closure does not add implicit close behavior.
Factories close newly acquired native resources when cancellation or an error prevents delivery. A with initializer registers successful acquisition before cancellation can unwind it. See completion and acquisition , sharing , and Closeable .

title: Concurrency
content:
Concurrency guide# Design index Concurrency is exposed through standard-library APIs. Ordinary calls run sequentially; every function can suspend. parallel runs related operations and joins them before returning. A Background service manages work with an explicitly chosen longer lifetime.
let [resA, resB] = try parallel(tasks: [first, second])The fragment belongs to a function returning Result[U, ExecutionError]; Unit tests match the result instead. See the complete error-adapting example .
Values are ordinary references. There are no source-level task handles, task moves, ownership transfers, or separate async function declarations. Closures snapshot local bindings; resource references remain subject to runtime closed-state checks.
Importing concurrency APIs# Concurrency adds no intrinsic names or compiler bounds. Import each API or type that the module names:
import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel_map from "@std/tasks.ms" import Background from "@std/tasks.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import OperationId from "@std/tasks.ms" import StartError from "@std/tasks.ms" import check_cancelled from "@std/tasks.ms" import Duration from "@std/time.ms"These are independent imports, not a required bundle. Importing one does not expose the others. Work status and failure reporting are also explicit standard exports; the standard API contract lists their paths. Ordinary Result annotations and error-adaptation helpers use their own imports from @std/result.ms.
Scheduling, cancellation, joining, time budgets, and service shutdown belong to these library/runtime APIs. The compiler checks callable sharing and the fixed parallel pack shape by the resolved standard binding identity. Its hidden execution context is an internal calling convention, not an ambient source capability or a new intrinsic type. A user function named parallel remains an ordinary function.
Fixed lifetimes# Every operation starts under a fixed execution lifetime. That relationship is chosen before work starts and does not change while it runs.
API Execution lifetime Ordinary call Current execution context parallel or parallel_map Joined group nested under the caller Background.start The chosen background service’s fixed host/component lifetime A helper may call parallel and return its completed result. It cannot return running work for another scope to adopt. Background work is started directly through the chosen service.
Passing a Background reference shares access to that service. It does not prolong the service’s lifetime, move its existing work, change its cancellation parent, or reset deadlines. The creating scope registers shutdown with with; aliases reject admission after closure.
A request can submit work through an application background service, but accepted work uses the service’s execution context. Request resources captured by that work can still close when the request exits; later use reports the resource’s closed-state error. Pass request data and application services, and acquire the operation’s resources inside it.
There is no task adoption, task reparenting, source-level detached work, or dynamic ownership graph. Scoped resources and ordinary references follow resource lifetimes .
Reading order# Parallel operations : calling parallel, argument preparation, and typed results Joined groups : the normative stop, join, and outcome contract for parallel and parallel_map Cancellation and budgets : cancellation requests, checkpoints, timeouts, and deadlines Runtime contracts : atomic transitions, resource acquisition, adapter contexts, and host escalation The standard library pages cover bounded parallel mapping and background services .

title: Parallel operations
content:
Parallel operations# Guide index · Design index parallel is a standard-library API for concurrent operations. Its named tasks argument receives functions to invoke, rather than already-running task handles. The API starts the operations and joins them before returning.
Calling parallel# import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" type User: id: Int type Order: id: Int type UserError: case Missing type OrderError: case Unavailable interface Users: fn get(id: Int) -> Result[User, UserError] interface Orders: fn for_user(user_id: Int) -> Result[List[Order], OrderError] type Summary: user: User orders: List[Order] type LoadError: case Execution(cause: ExecutionError) case UserFailure(cause: UserError) case OrderFailure(cause: OrderError) fn load(user_id: Int, users: Users & Shareable, orders: Orders & Shareable) -> Result[Summary, LoadError]: let first = fn() -> Result[User, UserError]: return users.get(id: user_id) let second = fn() -> Result[List[Order], OrderError]: return orders.for_user(user_id: user_id) let [resA, resB] = try map_error( result: parallel(tasks: [first, second]), transform: fn(cause: ExecutionError) -> LoadError: return LoadError.Execution(cause: cause) ) let user = try map_error( result: resA, transform: fn(cause: UserError) -> LoadError: return LoadError.UserFailure(cause: cause) ) let user_orders = try map_error( result: resB, transform: fn(cause: OrderError) -> LoadError: return LoadError.OrderFailure(cause: cause) ) return ok(value: Summary(user: user, orders: user_orders))Preparation# All arguments, pack entries, receivers, and captured snapshots are evaluated in written order in the caller, before entry into the API. In the example, first and second snapshot user_id and the shared services when constructed; their bodies run only after preparation succeeds and parallel starts the operations, inside the execution context parallel establishes.
If preparation fails, no operation has started. Preparation may have external effects; the runtime does not undo them. Resources acquired during preparation require their own with scopes or acquisition API contracts.
Passing users.get(...) instead of a function executes that call during preparation; it is not a way to schedule the call concurrently, and it is a type error when the result is not callable. Ordinary calls inside a function remain sequential unless another concurrency API is invoked.
Concurrent scheduling and external effect order are nondeterministic. Sharing a resource does not imply that simultaneous operations on it are semantically valid; its API must serialize access or report unsupported concurrent use. See closures and resource sharing .
Ordered, typed results# A literal task pack has a fixed number of positions. Each position accepts a zero-argument function and retains its individual return type. The successful result has the same shape and order: in the example, resA has type Result[User, UserError] and resB has type Result[List[Order], OrderError], regardless of completion order.
The brackets do not force these different types into a homogeneous List[T]. Fixed positional packs require type-system support for heterogeneous inputs and outputs; parallel itself remains an API call, with no special concurrency keyword. Ordinary list literals outside a positional-pack contract keep their homogeneous list rules.
Pack arity is preserved: parallel(tasks: [first]) returns a one-position successful result, destructured with let [resA] = ...; an empty pack returns an empty successful result and starts no work. Destructuring a fixed positional result with the wrong number of positions is a compile error. Parenthesized binding patterns such as let (resA, resB) = ... are not supported. See destructuring bindings .
Return values and errors# parallel returns an outer Result[Pack, ExecutionError]. The outer Result describes execution of the whole group. Each operation’s return value is preserved unchanged at its position:
Function returns Result position contains String String Result[Stock, OrderError] Result[Stock, OrderError] Optional[String] Optional[String] A returned domain error(cause: ...) is ordinary completion. It does not stop sibling operations and is not flattened into the outer Result. In the example, explicit map_error calls translate execution and domain errors into LoadError before each try; propagation still requires one exact error type. Matching each Result directly is also valid. There is no source task-result wrapper beyond the outer Result.
No operation remains running after parallel exits, on any path. An operation fault or an expired timeout stops and joins the group; caller cancellation joins the group and then unwinds the caller. The complete rules are in joined groups .
Results follow the ordinary reference rules ; returning a resource does not keep it open. Unreturned references become eligible for garbage collection; the runtime does not recursively close arbitrary results or captures. Resource cleanup comes from with or an acquisition-specific delivery contract. See completion and acquisition .
The optional named timeout argument shortens the inherited deadline; it never waives joining. See timeouts . Functions must meet the concurrent sharing contract . Use parallel_map for dynamic homogeneous inputs. The standard API contract fixes the callable/result mapping and legal uses of inferred packs; general source declaration syntax for packs is unsupported.

title: Joined groups
content:
Joined groups and execution outcomes# Guide index · Design index This page is the normative contract for joined groups created by parallel and parallel_map. Other pages link here rather than restate it.
Terms# Term Meaning Operation One invocation of a function passed to a concurrency API: a tasks position, one parallel_map item, or one Background.start submission Group The operations started by one parallel or parallel_map call Caller The execution that called the API; its context is the group’s fixed parent Joined Every started operation has finished its body and scope cleanup Execution errors# ExecutionError is exported by @std/tasks.ms; import it when naming the result type. Its Crashed payload uses OperationId, also exported by @std/tasks.ms. The standard declaration is:
type ExecutionError: case TimedOut case Crashed(operation: OperationId, message: String)OperationId identifies runtime work for diagnostics; it does not grant scheduling, joining, or transfer authority. Secondary faults are retained in runtime diagnostics associated with the primary outcome.
Group lifecycle# Prepare. The caller evaluates arguments in written order. If preparation fails, no operation starts. See preparation . Start. An empty pack or list returns ok immediately and starts no work, whatever the timeout. A zero timeout on nonempty input stops the group before any operation starts. Otherwise parallel starts every position and parallel_map keeps at most limit operations active. Stop. The first of these triggers stops the group: an operation faults, the group’s timeout expires, or the caller’s context is cancelled or reaches its inherited deadline. Stopping prevents further starts and requests cancellation of unfinished operations. Returning a domain error(cause: ...) is ordinary completion and never stops the group. Join. The API waits for every started operation, including its cleanup. Joining is not bounded by the timeout; uncooperative work falls to host escalation . Report. After joining, the caller observes the first matching row: Condition after joining Caller observes The caller’s own context was cancelled or reached its inherited deadline The caller unwinds; no Result is delivered. Operation faults become secondary diagnostics An operation faulted, in its body or cleanup error(cause: Crashed(...)) for the primary fault The group’s timeout expired before every operation committed error(cause: TimedOut) Otherwise ok(value: ...) with each operation’s exact return value in input order The first row is checked against the caller’s context, not the group’s derived context. Both can report an expired deadline; only the group’s own timer yields TimedOut, and only to a caller that is still active.
The primary fault is the first fault committed to the group’s outcome. When operations fault concurrently, which one is primary depends on scheduling. Successful value order never does. Commitment of an operation’s outcome and acceptance of a stop are atomic; an operation that committed before the stop keeps its outcome. See atomic transitions .
Faults are isolated at the group boundary# An operation fault becomes Crashed rather than unwinding the caller. This is intentional and matches how hosts isolate a failed request: the faulted operation has already unwound through its own cleanup, its siblings have been cancelled and joined, and the caller is the only remaining place that can respond. No faulted state is resumed. The caller’s own faults still unwind it; try propagates only Result errors.
No per-operation cancellation# No source or adapter API cancels a single operation of a joined group. An adapter that ends a foreign call early reports that through the operation’s declared return value, such as an IoError; it is not a fault. Joined APIs therefore have no separate cancelled outcome. Background work, which can be cancelled individually, reports cancellation through WorkStatus.Cancelled.
See parallel operations , cancellation , and scope cleanup .

title: Cancellation and budgets
content:
Cancellation and budgets# Guide index · Design index Cancellation follows fixed execution lifetimes. Request work inherits the request’s context; accepted background work inherits its background service’s context. A cancellation request asks work to stop; it does not establish that the work has stopped.
Requests# Hosts signal requests, joined groups signal their operations, and background services expose cancellation of admitted work:
let id = try background.start(operation: work) background.cancel(id: id)The submission fragment belongs to a function returning Result[U, StartError]; work must have the standard API contract callable type. Other application error types need explicit adaptation.
Successful Background.start admission yields an OperationId through Result[OperationId, StartError]. cancel(id: id) returns Unit, is idempotent for an admitted ID, and requests cancellation without joining. Dropping an ID has no effect. The service retains responsibility for work until it finishes or service shutdown joins it. IDs the service did not admit, including IDs from other services or from joined groups, and IDs whose status has been evicted are harmless no-ops; an ID never identifies unrelated work.
cancel, status, and close are receiver operations of the imported Background service; there are no ambient cancellation or join functions. Using an already-typed service does not require importing its otherwise unused type name. background.close() is the waiting boundary: it stops admission and performs the configured drain, cancellation, and joining sequence. A closed service stays closed through all aliases.
Late cancellation cannot overwrite an already committed completion. For background work, the first accepted stop reason determines WorkStatus, except that a programming fault during cleanup takes precedence and reports Crashed. Joined groups have no per-operation cancellation; their caller-visible outcomes are defined in joined groups .
Propagation and checkpoints# Cancellation is cooperative: stopped work unwinds at its next checkpoint. These are checkpoints:
runtime operation entry and completion; blocking I/O and other adapter calls; each loop back-edge, before the next iteration of for or while starts; an explicit check_cancelled() call. Loop checkpoints make CPU-bound loops respond promptly without source changes; they cost one poll of the context’s stop signal per iteration. check_cancelled() remains available for long straight-line work. It is an imported standard function, not a language intrinsic:
import check_cancelled from "@std/tasks.ms"Importing it supplies the operation declaration; the runtime supplies the current execution context when it is called. Cleanup runs under a shielded context, so checkpoints inside cleanup do not observe the initiating cancellation. No checkpoint occurs between with acquisition and cleanup registration; see completion and acquisition .
Cancelling a request or current operation cancels its nested groups. Each group joins its operations, each operation runs its registered with cleanup, and the caller unwinds.
Background service cancellation reaches the work admitted under that service. Cancellation of a submitting request does not cancel accepted work, because the background lifetime was selected at admission. Cancellation before admission must not start work. Admission and acknowledgement can race with request cancellation; callers must use application idempotency keys if a retried submission must not duplicate work.
Completed external writes remain completed. Cancellation does not provide rollback; a transaction’s explicit resource contract does.
Cleanup is shielded from the initiating cancellation and expired work deadline. It may exceed that deadline; it retains capability authority and remains subject to host escalation . See foreign cancellation and cleanup faults .
Timeouts# Timeouts are named library arguments, not syntax annotations. Duration values come from the standard time API; naming Duration requires its own import from @std/time.ms.
parallel(tasks: [first, second], timeout: 2.seconds) sets one budget for the group’s execution, starting on API entry after argument preparation. parallel_map supports the same option. timeout is the only budget argument; there is no absolute deadline argument.
Argument validation is part of the standard API contract ; zero-timeout and empty-input behavior is in joined groups . On expiry, the group stops, joins, and reports as defined in joined groups . Results are never delivered while work remains outstanding.
A timeout bounds ordinary work, not cleanup or joining. Foreign code that does not cooperate can delay joining indefinitely; host escalation is the final fallback. An API must not report successful joining merely because its timer expired.
To share one budget across several steps, put the steps in one function and give that function the budget. Nested groups inherit the deadline:
let sync = fn() -> Result[Unit, SyncError]: try download_all(sources: sources) try upload_all(targets: targets) return ok(value: unit) let [outcome] = try parallel(tasks: [sync], timeout: 2.seconds)This fragment requires an enclosing Result[U, ExecutionError] function; outcome is the unchanged Result[Unit, SyncError]. Any parallel or parallel_map inside download_all or upload_all inherits the same deadline.
Deadlines# Hosts establish deadlines for application, session, CLI, and request execution contexts. Every operation inherits its fixed parent’s deadline. A joined group can only shorten it with timeout; nothing in source can extend an inherited deadline. The effective deadline is the earliest of the inherited deadline and any group timeout.
Budgets use the runtime’s monotonic timer, not a Clock capability or calendar time. A test runner may virtualize that timer; a fake Clock value does not affect execution budgets.
When the caller’s own deadline expires, the caller unwinds after its groups join; it does not receive TimedOut. Only a group’s own timeout produces TimedOut.
Background work inherits the service’s fixed execution context, including that context’s deadline. It does not inherit the submitting request’s deadline. A service cannot revive cancelled work or extend its host’s deadline. Its context is selected at construction, not at each call to start.
Deadline configuration is a host operation. There are no source task handles to mutate, deadline annotations on functions, or absolute deadline arguments. See background services for drain budgets and adapter contexts .

title: Runtime contracts
content:
Runtime concurrency contracts# Guide index · Design index The runtime supplies starting, stopping, joining, and synchronization primitives. Library objects supply admission, failure reporting, and shutdown policy. These native primitives are internal implementation details. Source programs use explicit standard concurrency imports . The compiler validates resolved API typing, callable sharing, and cleanup contracts; runtime contexts and scheduler primitives add no intrinsic source names or bounds.
Atomic transitions# Each runtime operation has a stable OperationId, a fixed execution parent, a stop signal, an effective deadline, and one completion outcome. Cancellation acceptance and completion commitment have atomic linearization points. There is no reparenting or task-transfer transaction.
Background admission, closing admission, and reserving capacity must be coordinated atomically. If admission wins, the service tracks the accepted operation even if the submitting request stops before receiving its ID. If closure or cancellation wins before admission, the operation never starts. Capacity reservations are released exactly once: on rejection, or when the operation’s completion commits. Pending failure reports have their own bound and do not hold admission capacity.
Completion is not published until registered cleanup and nested joins have finished. A pending cancellation accepted before commitment prevents an ordinary successful outcome from being delivered. Already committed outcomes are stable.
User callbacks, failure reporters, resource cleanup, and joining run outside transition locks. Shutdown is idempotent; concurrent calls to close() observe one shutdown sequence and all wait for it to finish.
An operation must not join itself or an execution ancestor. Closing its own background service, including from nested parallel descendants or reporter callbacks joined by that service, faults before initiating shutdown. Check the fixed execution-parent chain, not just the current operation ID. Hosts close services from outside their admitted work. Cross-service cyclic shutdown is invalid library usage and must be avoided by host shutdown ordering.
The conformance suite uses controlled barriers and race stress for admission versus closure, cancellation versus completion, and concurrent shutdown. See semantic tests .
Completion and resource acquisition# Completion records an operation’s outcome after its body, nested concurrency groups, and registered cleanup finish. Cancellation and completion commitment race atomically; a late stop does not overwrite a committed outcome.
Parallel results are ordinary values, with references to existing objects where appropriate. If the group fails, unreturned references are released for garbage collection. The runtime does not recursively call close() on arbitrary result fields or closure captures: those references may alias resources still used elsewhere. Cleanup responsibility comes from explicit with registration or an acquisition API’s delivery contract, not a result-ownership escrow.
A native acquisition API must close a newly acquired resource if cancellation or a fault prevents it from being delivered. Successful acquisition and registration by with form one protected sequence: no cancellation checkpoint may occur between delivery to the binding and registration of its close() action.
Race outcome Required handling Cancellation wins before delivery Acquisition adapter closes the undelivered resource with acquires successfully Register cleanup before exposing cancellation Cancellation arrives after registration Unwind the scope and run registered cleanup Closure/result retains a resource reference after scope exit The reference remains valid memory; operations report that the resource is closed A source helper returning an open resource must handle resources it acquires but fails to return. Its resource factory/delivery contract is explicit. Merely returning a resource reference cannot cancel a with registration or keep the resource open.
Background operations have no resource-valued result delivery; each operation manages acquisitions through its own scopes. See adapter acquisition and resource release .
Adapter execution contexts# Generated calls carry a hidden execution context. An adapter observes the current operation’s fixed parent context, cancellation signal, deadline, and cleanup mode.
Parallel operations derive contexts from their caller. Background operations derive contexts from their service’s construction-time context. The runtime does not substitute the submitting request’s context merely because start was invoked from that request.
Fixed parent relationships can use Go context derivation directly; there is no movable cancellation ancestry or separate ownership graph. Operation IDs support diagnostics and traces. Go context documentation Cleanup receives a shielded context that ignores the initiating cancellation and expired ordinary-work deadline. It preserves authority; a host cleanup/escalation policy is separate from the request budget. Adapters must support safe resource closure and must not return from a cancelled operation while its foreign work is still outstanding.
See blocking adapters , deadlines , and runtime/library layering .
Host escalation# Joining and cleanup wait for work to actually end. The runtime cannot safely terminate an arbitrary goroutine, so work that ignores cancellation can delay a join forever. Escalation is the host’s last resort for that case. It ends the process; it never reports the stuck work as joined.
Each host runs one watchdog. It starts when the host begins shutdown or receives a stop request, such as SIGINT, SIGTERM, or server shutdown. Ordinary timeouts and request deadlines do not start it. Once started, it covers every waiting boundary: group joins, Background.close(), with cleanup, and resource close.
Setting Default Grace period after the stop request 30 seconds A second stop request during the grace period Escalates immediately Hosts may configure a different grace period. A zero grace period escalates on the first stop request whenever work is still outstanding.
On escalation the host:
writes one diagnostic per outstanding operation to host stderr, containing its OperationId, the source location of its current suspension, and its accepted stop reason; writes any retained primary and secondary fault diagnostics; terminates the process without running further cleanup. The CLI host exits 70 and labels the exit as incomplete cleanup. Conformance treats an escalated exit as a failure of the program, not as successful shutdown. See CLI exit and shutdown , HTTP shutdown , and cleanup faults .

Foreign adapter contracts # Adapter manifests Foreign values and the trust boundary Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition

title: Module boundaries
content:
Module boundaries# Guide index · Design index Identify visible declarations, imports, and the complete contract presented to callers.
Modules, exports, and imports Boundary contracts

title: Modules, exports, and imports
content:
Modules, exports, and imports# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A module defines which declarations belong together and which are available to other code.
Each .ms file is one module. Its resolved filesystem path identifies it; source files do not contain module declarations. Declarations are internal unless prefixed with export. Imports select individual exported symbols from explicit file paths; wildcard imports and cyclic module dependencies are rejected.
Names and declaration order# Types, interfaces, module functions, and imported symbols share one ordinary module namespace. Duplicate names, import/declaration collisions, and function overloading are rejected. Imports and declarations may appear in any order: collect names and signatures before checking bodies, so forward references and mutually recursive functions work. Type layout cycles follow the separate recursive data rule , not module-cycle rules.
The intrinsic core type names are only Bool, Int, Float, String, Unit, and Never. They cover primitive literals, ordinary arithmetic, and function/control-flow typing. The compiler bounds Shareable, Equal, and Hashable also have fixed identities. A module declaration, import, or type parameter cannot redefine these names. They are resolved names rather than lexical keywords. Ordinary local bindings may shadow outer names, but a shadowed value name cannot be used as a type.
All other standard declarations are explicit imports from the compiler-supplied @std directory, including Decimal, Bytes, collections, Optional, Result, Closeable, and runtime/host APIs. The standard imports and API typing page lists their modules. These names are ordinary exports: without an import, a module may declare its own Result, List, or parallel. Import/declaration collisions still fail. Compiler support follows the canonical standard declaration identity, never its spelling. Optional/Result case shorthand becomes visible when its alternative type is imported and follows ordinary lookup and ambiguity rules; qualify Result[T, E].error when a local spelling shadows it.
An unqualified case shorthand is considered only when ordinary lexical name lookup finds no binding or declaration of that name. The candidate cases come from visible alternative types declared in the module or imported by name. Exactly one candidate is required; an expected type cannot choose among multiple candidates. Type.Case explicitly selects the nominal alternative. Match-pattern case lookup uses the scrutinee type, as specified by pattern matching .
Import renaming, namespace imports, re-exports, and wildcard imports have no syntax. A dotted type path does not create a module namespace; callers import each needed exported type by its own name. Qualified alternative constructors remain supported. Module-level executable statements and bindings are rejected; local-value examples elsewhere are function-body fragments.
A visible contract# The file src/domain/customers.ms exports a nominal identifier type:
export type CustomerId: value: StringThe file src/main.ms imports the individual symbol:
import CustomerId from "./domain/customers.ms"Exporting a type makes it part of the module boundary; an internal declaration stays within that boundary. A relative import resolves from the importing file’s directory. Paths include the .ms extension and identify a file, with no implicit directory entry or extension lookup.
Public signature closure# An exported function, data type, or contract cannot expose an internal nominal type through a parameter, result, field, case payload, generic bound, or operation signature. Check the transitive public type surface through nested applications and exposed data members. Exported types from other modules may appear in a public signature without automatically re-exporting their names. Generic parameters themselves are not private nominal declarations.
type PrivateToken: value: String # Rejected: callers cannot name the internal result type. export fn issue() -> PrivateToken: return PrivateToken(value: "token")Exporting a record exposes every field and its constructor; exporting an alternative exposes every case and payload field; exporting an interface exposes every operation. Opaque exports and selective member visibility are unsupported. See public data surfaces .
An impl belongs to the receiver’s nominal data type’s defining module and becomes available when that module is loaded. Imported public contracts can be implemented there. Concrete and generic implementations do not re-export declarations. Duplicate or overlapping receiver/instantiated contract pairs are rejected, ignoring bounds when checking overlap; bounds cannot choose competing implementations. These coherence rules prevent behavior from depending on unrelated imports.
Standard-library imports# import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms"@std is always available without an [aliases] entry and cannot be overridden. Importing one export does not bring its signature’s other type names into scope. For example, importing parallel permits matching its inferred result, but writing Result or ExecutionError in an annotation requires their own imports. Importing a contract supplies its interface, not an authority-bearing value.
Optional aliases# A project-root ms.toml can define file and directory aliases. With @domain mapped to ./src/domain and @customers mapped to ./src/domain/customers.ms, either import selects the same exported type:
import CustomerId from "@domain/customers.ms"import CustomerId from "@customers"Each example is an alternative import spelling for the same CustomerId. Aliases change how a path is written; module identity and visibility still follow the resolved file. Relative imports and aliases that resolve to the same file refer to the same module.
Missing files, unknown aliases, missing exports, and cyclic module dependencies are compile errors. The project configuration defines alias resolution and filesystem identity.
See source structure and boundary contracts .
Next: Boundary contracts

title: Boundary contracts
content:
Boundary contracts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Review a module boundary by reading its exported types and operations, accepted capabilities, errors, sharing requirements, and resource lifetimes together. The compiler additionally derives external effects and call relationships.
Example: ordinary operations# The following uses application-defined Item, Stock, and OrderError types:
interface Inventory: fn check(items: List[Item]) -> Result[Stock, OrderError] fn check_stock( inventory: Inventory & Shareable, items: List[Item], ) -> Result[Stock, OrderError]: return inventory.check(items: items) let first = fn() -> Result[Stock, OrderError]: return check_stock(inventory: inventory, items: items) let [stock] = try parallel(tasks: [first])The closure/call fragment belongs to an enclosing function returning Result[U, ExecutionError]. To propagate OrderError in the same function, first translate it explicitly with map_error; parallel gives a complete example.
The operation accepts its capability explicitly and returns the unchanged domain Result. In this concurrent example the enclosing function’s inventory input has the shared Inventory & Shareable type, preserving the receiver proof in the captured capability and across check_stock’s parameter. A plain Inventory view would support sequential calls but could not be captured by this concurrent closure. The caller chooses concurrent execution through an ordinary API. The outer try handles execution failure; stock still contains the inventory domain outcome. The captured data must also meet the API’s sharing requirements.
Submitting work to a Background service instead chooses that service’s fixed lifetime. Passing a reference does not transfer cleanup or keep a scoped resource open.
See parallel operations , fixed work lifetimes , and derived effects .
Previous: Modules, exports, and imports · Next: Explicit capability authority

title: Authority and effects
content:
Authority and effects# Guide index · Design index Read explicit dependencies together with the external behavior inferred from them.
Explicit capability authority Inferred effects and call relationships

title: Explicit capability authority
content:
Explicit capability authority# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A capability is how external authority reaches Manuscript code. Read capability parameters to identify the services an operation can access.
Capabilities represent external authority such as storage, network access, a clock, or a model client. They are explicit inputs. Manuscript source has no ambient application access to these services. Standard shareable capability implementations support concurrent calls; shared internal state must be synchronized. Resource methods also enforce closed state.
The language requires explicit authority inputs. Tooling still needs a precise classification rule for distinguishing a capability interface from a pure operation contract, including wrappers and function values that retain authority. Until that rule is settled, a diagram cannot claim to enumerate all reachable authority from parameter names alone.
Sharing an implementation# A shareable network or storage implementation can receive concurrent calls. Its mutable internal state must be synchronized. References do not extend a resource’s open lifetime; methods coordinate active calls with close.
Passing a capability explicitly makes the dependency visible to reviewers and compiler-derived diagrams. It also makes it possible to substitute controlled implementations when testing.
See resource sharing and the foreign-code trust boundary .
Previous: Boundary contracts · Next: Inferred effects and call relationships

title: Inferred effects and call relationships
content:
Inferred effects and call relationships# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Effects describe behavior reachable through an operation, including behavior performed by its callees.
Effects are inferred transitively. Foreign adapters supply declared effect summaries. The effect vocabulary is read, write, external-call, and unknown. An unresolved function-value or contract call contributes unknown, never an empty effect set. Known targets contribute their union. A contract reports reachable behavior; Manuscript has no source effect-bound syntax or static purity promise. Foreign code is trusted to honor its summaries. External writes are not reversible through cancellation.
Transitive analysis# A function calling an operation that writes externally inherits that external effect in the derived summary. Foreign adapters must declare summaries because source analysis cannot inspect their behavior as ordinary Manuscript calls.
Cancellation can stop unfinished work and trigger cleanup, but it cannot undo an external write that has already completed. A review of a boundary must therefore consider effects as well as returned errors.
See diagram views and architecture changes .
Previous: Explicit capability authority · Next: Adapter manifests

title: Foreign adapter contracts
content:
Foreign adapter contracts# Guide index · Design index Specify how Go implementations preserve source values, cancellation, and explicit resource cleanup and closed-state safety.
Adapter manifests Foreign values and the trust boundary Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition

title: Adapter manifests
content:
Adapter manifests# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Adapters are trusted Go implementations of operation contracts, exposed through plain or shared views according to their declared receiver-sharing guarantee. The standard API contract is normative for standard APIs; a manifest implements rather than invents their source semantics.
Interface modules and package direction# A local adapter ships a .ms interface module containing exported data and contracts, with no function bodies, tests, or implementation blocks. It may import standard modules through @std/...ms and other registered interface modules. Signatures use intrinsic types, explicitly imported standard types, or public declarations in that interface graph, never application-defined types. Source imports interface declarations through ordinary .ms paths.
Each interface module generates a separate Go schema package. The native adapter imports schemas and runtime; the application imports schemas, adapters, and runtime. Schemas never import adapters or application packages. Standard schemas belong to the pinned standard-library/runtime distribution. This prevents Go import cycles. An application contract over application Money types can have source implementations or explicitly wrap an adapter interface using data conversion, but cannot directly bind a separately compiled native adapter to application types.
Native receivers remain opaque. The host creates them and exposes contract views. Source fakes implement the interface contract for their own concrete type under ordinary coherence. The standard CLI host supplies only its enumerated roots; custom host construction still needs a concrete contract.
Manifest version 1# The manifest is UTF-8 TOML with closed fields; unknown keys, duplicate bindings, unsupported versions, missing fields, and signature mismatches are compile errors.
format = 1 interface = "./files.ms" go_package = "example.org/nativefiles" go_version = "v1.0.0" go_checksum = "h1:example-content-checksum" [[bindings]] contract = "Files" operation = "open" symbol = "Open" effects = ["read", "external-call"] shareable_receiver = true cancellation = "cooperative" acquisition = "dispose-undelivered" disposer = "DisposeFile"This is a schema example; its package and checksum are placeholders. Interface paths resolve relative to the manifest, and the Go fields pin the native package.
Binding field Rule contract, operation, symbol Select an exported interface/standard contract operation and an exported Go symbol; bind each operation exactly once effects Explicit subset of read, write, external-call, and unknown; use [] for an empty summary shareable_receiver Required audited boolean, consistent across the receiver’s operations; true permits shared views, false permits only plain views cancellation cooperative, completion-only, or nonblocking acquisition none or dispose-undelivered disposer Required exported symbol for dispose-undelivered; forbidden for none Resource bindings include a matching close operation. A standard host boundary requiring sharing rejects a nonshareable receiver. Source code can still explicitly discard a native receiver’s sharing guarantee by constructing a plain view.
Generated bindings# Interface declarations determine parameter labels/order and result types; manifests do not duplicate them. Each Go operation receives the hidden execution context, opaque receiver, and generated parameters in declaration order, then returns the generated exact result type.
A disposer receives a shielded context and the acquired generated resource value. It completes release before returning. The fixed constructor New accepts runtime HostInputs and returns an opaque receiver token. Standard host packages follow the same convention.
The concrete Go declarations for HostInputs, receiver tokens, results, and disposers still need a pinned runtime ABI. Symbol/type mismatches must fail validation before linking; referring to an ABI alone does not define those declarations.
Wrappers enforce the foreign value invariants . Disposal of an undelivered acquisition finishes before unwind, and no wrapper returns with outstanding foreign work. Native code requires separate cancellation, sharing, conversion, and release tests.
Acceptance requires a minimal interface/native-adapter/application fixture whose Go builds without cycles, rejection of interface imports from the application, source fake implementations, and invalid-value/acquisition race fixtures.

title: Foreign values and the trust boundary
content:
Foreign values and the trust boundary# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Adapter conversion must preserve the source language’s value invariants when data crosses the Go boundary.
Adapters validate UTF-8, alternative tags and payloads, required non-nil values, and numeric ranges. They preserve immutability and copy buffers unless exclusive ownership can be established. Mutable Go storage, unrestricted Go interfaces, and runtime task internals are not exposed to Manuscript source. Raw Go dependencies may use ambient authority, so source capability checking is not a sandbox for adapter code.
Preserving invariants# A converted string must be valid UTF-8. An alternative must carry a valid tag. A buffer must not become mutable through a hidden Go alias after being exposed as immutable source data. Exclusive native buffer transfer is an optimization only when the adapter proves no mutable Go aliases remain; source code has no move or ownership checker.
An invalid foreign value is a programming fault with the operation, expected type, and value path in its diagnostic. It is not an expected input error: untrusted data should remain Bytes until explicitly decoded. The manifest binding defines wrapper validation and release obligations.
See Go representations and text and byte values .
Previous: Adapter manifests · Next: Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition

title: Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition
content:
Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A blocking adapter must connect the operation’s stable execution context to the underlying operation and report when its outstanding work has actually ended.
Each blocking adapter defines how cancellation reaches the underlying operation and when cleanup completes. An uncancellable foreign call remains outstanding until it finishes; wrapping it in a goroutine and returning early violates joining guarantees. Host escalation is the final fallback. Adapters report acquired resources even when cancellation races with acquisition, so the runtime can close newly acquired undelivered resources.
An acquisition race# Suppose a connection is acquired just as cancellation is accepted. The acquisition adapter must close it if delivery loses the race. Once delivered into with, cleanup registration has no intervening cancellation checkpoint. This contract applies to newly acquired resources, not arbitrary result references that may alias existing objects.
See stable adapter contexts and result commitment .

title: Compilation pipeline
content:
Compilation pipeline# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The compiler design translates Manuscript source into Go while enforcing source contracts that Go alone does not supply. This is an implementation contract for the future compiler.
The compiler is implemented in Go. Parsing, type, scope, and capture checking produce typed intermediate representation with explicit evaluation order, closure captures, cleanup scopes, effects, and source locations. The backend emits one application Go package plus separate adapter interface schema packages, using versioned runtime/native capability packages, then invokes a pinned Go toolchain. Schema packages cannot depend on the application; adapter bindings define the acyclic package direction.
Following a program through compilation# The compiler first reads the project’s ms.toml, loads its entry .ms file, and discovers modules through relative path imports and optional aliases. Canonical resolved file paths establish module identity. Parsing establishes source structure without module declarations. Import checking resolves exported symbols and rejects dependency cycles; type, scope, and capture checking resolve source types, captures, and scopes. The typed representation records the facts lowering needs to preserve. Emitting and building the application uses the separately versioned runtime and adapters.
The design specifies this pipeline, but does not establish a concrete parser library, AST schema, or internal package layout.
See project configuration and module paths , type checking , scope and capture checking , and the typed representation .
Next: Type checking and source contracts

title: Type checking and source contracts
content:
Type checking and source contracts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The type checker enforces the core language’s declared contracts before Go emission. A Go representation is not sufficient evidence that a source operation is legal.
Required checks# Accept source according to the normative grammar ; then resolve names and check the compatibility rules . Each rejected program must identify the violated source rule. Backend assignability and Go compiler acceptance are not substitutes for those checks.
Source rule Checker responsibility Explicit function signatures Check parameter and result types against calls and returns Names and scopes Collect module signatures, reject duplicate names, resolve locals in declaration order, and check assignments against fixed mutable binding types Operators Use the closed precedence and operand table; enforce Bool conditions and short-circuit evaluation without implicit numeric conversion Function values Preserve parameter labels/order and exact types; require explicit specialization of generic function values and explicit anonymous signatures Return completeness Allow Unit fallthrough/bare returns; reject reachable non-Unit fallthrough; track Never and function-local loop/return boundaries Mandatory argument names Reject unnamed, unknown, duplicate, or missing required call arguments and match names to declared parameters, including function-value calls List literals Require the canonical standard List import; check homogeneous shareable element types and use annotations or the expected parameter type for empty lists Parallel API packs Check zero-argument functions in literal tasks: [...] packs and preserve each position’s exact return type; see parallel operations Destructuring bindings Check positional arity, record fields, renaming, nesting, and duplicate bindings; infer each local’s type independently; see destructuring bindings Nominal records and tagged alternatives Preserve type identity and check declared fields and cases Expected types Propagate annotations/substituted constructor context through literals, fields, and parentheses; reject incomplete types and avoid result-context inference for generic calls Exhaustive match Check the scrutinee alternative, positional payload arity/bindings, exact qualified cases, missing alternatives, duplicate arms, and final nonredundant wildcard Generic bounds Check arity, invariant arguments, argument-only inference, every nested application’s bounds, and generic bodies under their declared assumptions Recursive types and specialization Reject inline storage cycles and expanding generic type/function specialization, including mutual calls and specialized function values; permit regular recursion guarded by immutable collection storage Equality and hashing Derive only the specified properties; reject Float/collection keys and data containing ineligible components Explicit implementations Match substituted operation names/labels/order/types exactly, check generic bodies and receiver-determined parameters, reject overlap ignoring bounds, enforce defining-module coherence, and require explicit contract views Standard bindings and sharing Resolve the minimal intrinsic prelude and explicit standard imports by canonical declaration identity, distinguish plain and shared contract views, require receiver sharing proof only for shared views, reject implicit guarantee removal or recovery, and retain callable sharing proofs independently of function signature identity Public signatures Reject internal nominal types leaking through exported fields, signatures, bounds, or operation surfaces Iteration Admit List/Set/Map only, bind immutable element/MapEntry types, evaluate iterable once, and reject loop control outside the current function’s loops Result propagation Recognize the canonical standard Result identity; require the same exact error type at a try expression in the current function; do not infer missing operand type arguments backward String literals Validate escape/scalar syntax, check interpolated scalar eligibility, and preserve left-to-right evaluation These requirements derive from the core language guide , with accepted and rejected modules in core conformance . The rules specify observable inference and compatibility; checker data structures and internal pass organization remain implementation choices. A module-level test body is a zero-parameter Unit function for static checking: ordinary local scopes, bare-return/fallthrough rules, and Result propagation restrictions apply. Test discovery and runner execution remain separate tooling contracts.
Type information feeds typed IR , generated representations , and structural tools .

title: Scope and capture checking
content:
Scope and closure checking# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The frontend validates cleanup registration and closure captures without a general ownership or lifetime checker.
Source operation Required check with initializer Require the concrete, contract-view, or generic-bound proof defined by Closeable ; register the resolved operation Scope exit Identify exited cleanup scopes for return, loop exits, errors, faults, and cancellation Closure creation Identify captured bindings and snapshot them once Assignment to captured outer local Reject implicit shared mutable cells Reassignment and branch scope Require initializers, enforce let/var, and keep branch-local names inside their scope Concurrency eligibility Retain type-level sharing through generic data/shared-contract boundaries; check callable value proofs separately at standard API entry Callable proof erasure Retain safe local capture proofs for direct standard callable arguments; erase them through generic forwarding, fields, and source function parameter/result boundaries; function types never satisfy Shareable Call-only standard bindings For resolved standard declaration identities only, reject extracting parallel, parallel_map, Background constructors, or Background.start as function/bound-method values; validate every direct call’s required callable proofs. Same-spelled application functions follow ordinary function-value rules Capturing a scoped resource is not a compile error merely because it may outlive its scope. Methods report closed state at runtime. Storing or returning a reference does not transfer a cleanup action. There are no moved-binding states, borrow lifetimes, partial-move restrictions, or source task-ownership checks.
See with scopes , closures , and typed IR .

title: Typed intermediate representation
content:
Typed intermediate representation# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The intermediate representation carries the checked program into lowering and supplies facts used by tooling.
Fact Why it remains explicit Types, sharing bounds, and resolved operations Preserve plain/shared contract identity, receiver-sharing proofs, and substituted generic implementation selection; select representations and validate API contracts Argument names and parameters Preserve named-call checking and written evaluation order Lists and fixed positional packs Retain homogeneous element types or each position’s exact type Destructuring Retain shapes, field bindings, and extraction order Closure environments Record snapshot captures and receiver references with registration and cleanup scopes Resolve close() and unwind exited scopes Effects and concurrency API boundaries Derive host/service relationships and diagrams Source locations Connect generated behavior back to source There are no ownership-transfer instructions or affine states. Runtime operation IDs and fixed execution parents belong to the concurrency runtime; source IR records the API calls and contexts used to establish them.
