title: Function and concurrency API lowering
content:
Function and concurrency API lowering# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Ordinary functions, closures, and contract methods become Go calls with a hidden execution-context parameter. Closures have environments containing their snapshot captures. Source signatures retain one function kind; every function can suspend.
Explicitly imported parallel, parallel_map, and Background methods lower as typed library calls. Scheduling, cancellation, joining, admission, and shutdown policy live in the standard library/runtime rather than an expanded source intrinsic list. Native runtime primitives start goroutines, signal cancellation, join completion, and synchronize state. The compiler checks the resolved standard API declarations and their callable-proof requirements; a same-spelled application declaration acquires none of that special typing. There is no special background class or task transfer. Go concurrency specification The hidden context carries the current operation, fixed cancellation parent, effective deadline, and cleanup mode. Parallel operations derive it from the caller; a background service supplies its stored construction-time context. Creating a closure does not capture the caller’s execution context as a hidden source dependency; invocation supplies the execution context. Each loop back-edge polls the context’s stop signal and unwinds through the iteration’s cleanup if it has stopped; cleanup contexts are shielded, so the poll never fires during cleanup.
The frontend implements the standard library’s fixed heterogeneous callable/result mapping , preserving inferred packs through locals, generic helpers, and Result matches. This is type-system/interop support for the API. General source pack syntax is unsupported; the standard mapping is normative and cannot be altered by an adapter manifest.
Policy can be implemented over native primitives. No goroutine-ID lookup, custom coroutine lowering, stack implementation, or memory collector is required. See parallel and background layering .

title: Source guarantees and Go representations
content:
Source guarantees and Go representations# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Representations must implement the checked source behavior, including guarantees absent from unrestricted Go values.
The frontend enforces semantics that Go representations do not provide:
Source guarantee Go lowering Checked Int int64 with checked operations and conversions Decimal Versioned finite decimal implementation honoring the coefficient/exponent grid, exact literals, and per-operator rounding in the numeric contract Valid UTF-8 String Validated construction and conversion; no raw string escape Immutable bytes and collections Encapsulated storage; copies or exclusive adapter transfer Ordered maps and sets Ordered wrappers Tagged alternatives Generated typed tags and payloads; exhaustive frontend checking Guarded recursive data Inline records/alternatives with immutable container indirection; reject invalid layouts before Go emission Value equality and hashing Generated operations for eligible types Explicit contract implementation Frontend selection of a unique applicable concrete/generic implementation, then Go interfaces and wrappers Closures and resource references GC-retained environments, snapshot captures, and synchronized native closed-state checks Lexical cleanup Explicit with registrations, shielded Closeable.close(), and scope unwind operations Parallel results Typed positional packs preserving each exact return value Use Go generics where suitable; generated typed pack wrappers handle heterogeneous parallel results without exposing unchecked casts to source.
Representation boundaries# For example, emitting a raw int64 does not supply checked arithmetic. A raw Go slice does not establish immutable source bytes. The frontend and runtime cooperate with generated wrappers and operations to preserve those contracts.
Explicit view constructors create contract wrappers. Plain and shared views may use the same runtime representation, while the frontend and IR retain distinct identities and sharing proofs. Go interface assignment or runtime receiver inspection cannot restore an erased proof.
Generic implementation bodies use checked substitutions; Go method selection cannot resolve overlapping source implementations. Function wrappers retain source labels/order in frontend identity even though Go erases labels. Check recursive storage rules before emission; a generated-Go error is not a source type check.
Int division/remainder overflow handling, Float non-finite outcomes, Decimal underflow/overflow, and checked truncation conversions follow runtime numeric outcomes , including parameterized runtime operands. Unchecked Go casts or a decimal package’s defaults do not establish these semantics.
See foreign conversions , type checking , and scope and capture checking .

title: Evaluation order and call preparation
content:
Evaluation order and call preparation# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Resolve each source argument name to its parameter, evaluate arguments into temporaries in written order, then arrange Go parameters. Preserve short-circuit control flow.
A tasks: [...] literal constructs a typed pack of function values in source order. Constructing closures snapshots their local captures; it does not invoke their bodies. If preparation fails, the concurrency API has not started work. Native acquisitions during preparation retain their explicit delivery/cleanup contracts.
Ordinary list elements evaluate left to right; an existing list argument evaluates once. Destructuring evaluates the initializer once and extracts bindings in written pattern order, retaining each positional result type.
A with initializer evaluates once, then registers the initialized object’s resolved close method before exposing another cancellation checkpoint. Later alias assignment does not change that receiver.
See source call order , operation preparation , and with scopes .

title: Cleanup and fault lowering
content:
Cleanup and fault lowering# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Generated cleanup registers Closeable.close() for successful with initialization and explicitly unwinds exited block scopes. Go’s function-level defer alone does not represent nested-block and iteration lifetimes.
The backend implements scope-exit order and fault selection as follows:
Use private tagged Go panics for nonlocal language faults and cancellation. Give each function with active registrations a local scope stack and one deferred unwind handler. Normal block exits drain and pop explicitly; panic paths drain the remaining stack. Pop an action before invoking it, and recover each close separately so a secondary panic cannot skip later cleanup. Give cleanup a context without the initiating cancellation or expired work deadline, retaining authority and cleanup mode. Rethrow the selected fault or cancellation after draining, until its operation or host boundary handles it. Recoverable unexpected adapter panics become programming faults; concurrency boundaries report them as Crashed. Active parallel APIs join before the caller’s cleanup begins. Ordinary values and captures are never recursively disposed. Process-fatal out-of-memory or stack exhaustion has no cleanup guarantee.
Resources acquired but not delivered require cleanup from the acquisition adapter or factory. Returned references do not suppress an existing with registration. See exit order , fault selection , and acquisition races .

title: Builds and dependencies
content:
Builds and dependencies# Guide index · Design index Configure projects and module paths, pin identities, generate stable output, and respect Go package compilation boundaries.
Project configuration and module paths Pinned dependencies and deterministic output Caching and Go package boundaries

title: Project configuration and module paths
content:
Project configuration and module paths# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A project has an ms.toml file at its root. The compiler reads this file to locate source and the entry file and to resolve optional import aliases. Each .ms file is one module; no source-level module declaration is required or accepted.
A project manifest# [project] name = "store" source = "./src" entry = "./src/main.ms" [aliases] "@domain" = "./src/domain" "@customers" = "./src/domain/customers.ms"project.name names the project. project.source identifies its source directory, and project.entry identifies its entry .ms file. All filesystem paths in the manifest resolve relative to the directory containing ms.toml, including the entry path; the entry path is not relative to project.source.
Commands and module discovery# Command Behavior ms check <ms.toml> Check the program and its entry signature ms build <ms.toml> Check, generate Go, and build the executable A relative manifest argument resolves from the invocation directory. Its containing directory then becomes the project root for configuration paths. The entry follows the CLI main contract .
The compiler discovers application modules by following imports from entry. The manifest does not enumerate them. Optional [adapters] entries map identifiers to project-relative manifest paths, for example files = "./adapters/files.toml". Adapter bindings define their interfaces and native symbols. Unknown manifest tables or keys are rejected.
The compiler supplies the minimal intrinsic prelude and the standard modules under @std, alongside local adapter interfaces. Third-party Manuscript packages are unsupported; native dependencies follow build pinning .
Resolving an import# Imports name an exported symbol and a path:
import CustomerId from "./domain/customers.ms" import Order from "@domain/orders.ms"For an import in src/main.ms, the first path resolves to src/domain/customers.ms. The second expands @domain using the manifest and resolves to src/domain/orders.ms.
A path beginning with ./ or ../ resolves relative to the importing file’s directory. A path beginning with @std/ resolves within the compiler-supplied standard-library directory. @std alone selects no module. The [aliases] key @std is rejected, so an application cannot override standard identities. Other paths beginning with @ resolve through the importing project’s aliases. Alias keys consist of @ followed by one identifier, such as @domain. A directory alias matches its complete first path segment and appends the remaining path. @domain does not match @domain_extra. A directory alias alone does not select a module. A file alias selects exactly its target .ms file and accepts no appended path segments. Alias targets are filesystem paths relative to ms.toml; aliases do not expand other aliases. Direct paths and paths appended to directory aliases must include .ms. Resolution does not infer extensions or search for directory entry files. A file alias can omit the extension in the import because its configured target supplies it. Bare logical module names and absolute filesystem paths are not import forms. Paths use / as the separator. [aliases] is optional. Ordinary relative imports work without it. Missing source directories or entry files, invalid alias definitions, unknown aliases, and imports that do not resolve to an existing .ms file are compile errors. Import checking also rejects missing or internal symbols, wildcard imports, and cyclic module dependencies.
Module identity and configuration scope# The compiler normalizes resolved paths, including . and .., and resolves symbolic links to establish one canonical file identity within a build. Importing the same file through a relative path, a file alias, or a directory alias does not create separate modules. Cycle detection and module caching use this identity, so alternate path spellings cannot bypass cycle checks. Stable build metadata records paths relative to the owning project root rather than checkout-specific absolute paths.
Application paths, source directories, user aliases, adapter manifests, and interface modules must resolve inside the project root after symlink resolution. Escapes are compile errors. @std/...ms is the sole exception: paths resolve inside the pinned standard-library directory, and normalization/symlinks cannot escape that directory or reach application files. Standard module identity is its distribution version/content identity plus canonical distribution-relative path, independent of its installation location. Standard modules cannot import application modules. Interfaces may use intrinsic types and import standard declarations or other registered interfaces, never application modules. Native Go dependencies are pinned adapter inputs. External Manuscript dependency projects and package acquisition syntax are unsupported.
Changes to source roots, entry files, aliases, or the pinned standard-library distribution can change the resolved module graph. The compiler includes relevant manifest settings in build and analysis cache identity, alongside source and dependency identities.
See module exports and imports , the compilation pipeline , and incremental compilation .

title: Pinned dependencies and deterministic output
content:
Pinned dependencies and deterministic output# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A build’s identity includes the source, relevant ms.toml settings, toolchain, runtime, adapters, and dependencies used to produce it. The project manifest establishes the entry file, source directory, and optional import aliases.
Pin the Go toolchain, compiler-supplied standard-library modules and their content identity, runtime, native adapters, and their dependencies. @std resolves only to that pinned distribution; a build does not fetch or silently substitute a newer library. Include this identity in module, analysis, and generated-code caches. Debug builds also pin the supported Delve version.
Generate deterministic symbol names and declaration order; do not rewrite unchanged output. This promises stable generated source for the same inputs. Byte-identical binaries need a separate toolchain and environment contract.
Details still needed# ms lock ms.toml explicitly creates or updates project-root ms.lock, a JSON object with closed fields: format: 1, compiler: "0.1.0", implementation_sha256, and toolchain. The implementation digest covers sorted compiler/frontend and embedded runtime source contents, excluding tests and checkout paths. Toolchain records Go version, OS/architecture, CGO, experiments, and architecture tuning from the selected MANUSCRIPT_GO. Pinned builds require empty GOFLAGS and use explicit -trimpath; --debug additionally disables optimization and inlining.
Project build, run, and test reject missing or mismatched pins and instruct the caller to explicitly run lock. Check/format/inspect/emit do not require a native toolchain pin. Standalone module builds record the selected toolchain without claiming a project lock. There are no third-party native dependencies in the supplied runtime. External adapter dependency pins and Delve remain separate future distribution contracts.
Native artifacts are cached under project .ms-cache/ by generated source, original module/configuration hashes, implementation content, target/toolchain, and debug flags. Cache hits verify metadata and binary content hashes; corruption rebuilds. A matching output is not rewritten. <executable>.ms-build.json carries source/configuration hashes and executable identity. compiler.VerifyBuild rejects mismatched binaries or supplied source/configuration snapshots before source interpretation. This pins source generation and artifact identity; byte-identical binary reproducibility across environments is not promised.
Pinning Delve keeps the native transport contract aligned with debugger integration .
Build identity and source hashes must travel with debug and trace metadata . See incremental compilation for caching and package boundaries.
Previous: Project configuration and module paths · Next: Caching and Go package boundaries

title: Caching and Go package boundaries
content:
Caching and Go package boundaries# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Incremental work has two boundaries: compiler analysis can reuse source-derived summaries, while Go rebuilds at package granularity.
Cache parsing, checking, and module summaries by source, relevant project configuration, and dependency identity. Use canonical resolved file identity for modules; imports through different path spellings or aliases share a module summary.
Runtime, adapter schemas, and native adapters compile as separate packages. Native adapters and the application import schemas; schemas never import either. Adapter interfaces cannot use application types. Changing application code rebuilds its package; multiple generated files do not create independent compilation units. Go build documentation See project configuration , the pipeline , and deterministic generation .

title: Conformance and scope
content:
Conformance and scope# Guide index · Design index Validate individual guarantees and complete programs across the language, runtime, and tools.
Core-language conformance fixtures Runtime binding acceptance cases Semantic conformance tests Complete-program conformance Scope and implementation order

title: Core-language conformance fixtures
content:
Core-language conformance fixtures# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index These fixtures specify acceptance, rejection, and evaluation for the core language. They supplement the semantic conformance plan ; they do not specify a test runner, executable host, ownership, or concurrency.
Each fenced accepted fixture is an independent .ms module, with its application types and helper functions included. Its module-level test body has the ordinary Unit return contract. A rejected variant replaces or removes exactly the indicated text in that fixture, leaving the rest unchanged. If a variant introduces a standard declaration, add its individual import unless missing-import rejection is the behavior under test. Test each variant independently: combining unrelated errors makes the expected diagnostic ambiguous.
The expected stage identifies the violated contract: parse for invalid source structure; resolution for an unknown or ambiguous symbol; type for incompatible types, shapes, labels, bounds, or control flow after parsing and resolution. A checker may combine its resolution and type passes, but must identify the specified cause at the offending source span. Diagnostic wording and internal pass layout are implementation choices. Accepted fixtures must evaluate to the stated assertions, rather than merely generate Go that compiles.
CL-01: Layout and named-call syntax# Contract: source syntax and declarations and calls .
fn subtract(amount: Int, deduction: Int) -> Int: return amount - deduction test "named multiline call": let remaining = subtract( deduction: 2, amount: 9, ) assert remaining == 7This accepts trailing commas and multiline calls while mapping labels to declared parameters. Reordering the written labels does not change the parameter mapping.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the call with subtract(amount: 9, deduction: 2) Accept; remaining is Int and equals 7 Replace it with subtract(9, 2) Parse rejection: supplied arguments require names Replace it with subtract(amount: 9, amount: 2) Type rejection: duplicate supplied argument and missing deduction Replace it with subtract(amount: 9) Type rejection: missing required deduction Replace it with subtract(amount: 9, discount: 2) Type rejection: unknown argument name discount Replace return amount - deduction with return missing Resolution rejection: unknown binding missing Remove the indentation before the function’s return Parse rejection: missing function block/module-level return Add lexical rejection fixtures for tabs, inconsistent dedentation, and unterminated delimiters as specified by the syntax chapter. Preserve the error’s actual cause rather than reporting a later missing return.
CL-02: Arithmetic grouping and Boolean short-circuiting# Contract: expressions and operators and numeric operations .
fn invalid_division(zero: Int) -> Bool: return 1 / zero == 0 test "grouping and short circuit": assert 2 + 3 * 4 == 14 assert (2 + 3) * 4 == 20 assert 10 - 3 - 2 == 5 assert true or invalid_division(zero: 0) assert not (false and invalid_division(zero: 0))Both short-circuit assertions must complete without invoking the invalid division. This observes control flow, not only operator result types.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace 2 + 3 * 4 with 2 + 3.0 * 4.0 Type rejection: mixed Int and Float, without implicit conversion Replace true or invalid_division(zero: 0) with 1 or invalid_division(zero: 0) Type rejection: logical operand must be Bool Replace a comparison with 1 < 2 < 3 Parse rejection: comparison operators cannot chain Replace true or invalid_division(zero: 0) with true or panic(message: "skipped") Accept and evaluate to true: the skipped Never operand is admissible as Bool Replace false and invalid_division(zero: 0) with false and panic(message: "skipped") Accept and evaluate to false: the right Never operand is not evaluated Integer overflow and division-by-zero fixtures must expect programming faults even if the backend could evaluate a wrapping Go operation. Use parameterized helpers to exercise runtime inputs rather than relying only on constant folding. Literal-range rejection is a separate compile-time fixture.
CL-03: Nominal constructors and record bindings# Contract: records and destructuring .
type CustomerId: value: String type OrderId: value: String type Customer: id: CustomerId name: String fn customer_name(customer: Customer) -> String: let {id: {value}, name: display_name} = customer return "{value}: {display_name}" test "nominal record and nested binding": let customer = Customer(id: CustomerId(value: "c1"), name: "Ada") assert customer_name(customer: customer) == "c1: Ada" Independent variant Expected outcome Use OrderId(value: "c1") for the customer’s id Type rejection: nominal OrderId is not CustomerId Omit name in Customer(...) Type rejection: missing field Add active: true to Customer(...) Type rejection: unknown field Supply name twice Type rejection: duplicate field Bind {email} from customer Type rejection: unknown record field Bind {id: value, name: value} Type rejection: duplicate local binding Assign customer.name = "Grace" after construction Parse rejection: assignment accepts a binding name, not a field target Public-surface rejection fixture:
import List from "@std/collections.ms" type PrivateId: value: String export type PublicRecord: ids: List[PrivateId]Reject at type checking: the exported field exposes the internal nominal PrivateId through a nested application. Changing type PrivateId to export type PrivateId accepts the module. Public closure is not satisfied merely because the outer standard List type is public.
CL-04: Positional bindings and list shape# Contract: collections and destructuring .
import List from "@std/collections.ms" fn difference(values: List[Int]) -> Int: let [first, second] = values return first - second test "list binding": assert difference(values: [9, 4]) == 5 let empty: List[Int] = [] let {value: label} = Label(value: "ready") assert label == "ready" type Label: value: StringThe empty literal gets its type from the annotation. difference’s binding is checked against List[Int]; its exact length is validated when the function runs.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace [9, 4] with [9, 4.0] Type rejection: heterogeneous numeric list without explicit conversion Replace let empty: List[Int] = [] with let empty = [] Type rejection: insufficient element-type information Replace the binding with let (first, second) = values Parse rejection: parenthesized positional binding is unsupported Replace the test call with difference(values: [9]) Function accepts List[Int]; evaluation faults at dynamic destructuring Replace the empty declaration with let [only] = [1, 2] Type rejection: statically known length mismatch; no extra value is discarded Annotate let [first, second]: List[Int] = values Parse rejection: only simple name bindings accept annotations A literal-length mismatch in the binding itself is a compile-time shape error; a list parameter’s runtime length is a programming-fault check. Optional optimization must not turn acceptance of the parameterized function into an invented fixed-length parameter type.
CL-05: Function values retain parameter labels# Contract: function values .
fn increase(value: Int) -> Int: return value + 1 fn apply(value: Int, transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int) -> Int: return transform(value: value) test "function label compatibility": let transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int = increase assert apply(value: 4, transform: transform) == 5 Independent variant Expected outcome Rename only increase’s parameter and body binding to item Type rejection: fn(item: Int) -> Int is incompatible with fn(value: Int) -> Int Call transform(item: value) in apply Type rejection: unknown function-value argument label Change increase to return Float with body return 1.0 Type rejection at assignment/call: function result contract differs Change it to return Never with body panic(message: "stop") Type rejection at assignment: Never expression compatibility does not make function result types covariant Change the apply call to omit transform Type rejection: required function argument is missing CL-06: Return completeness and Boolean conditions# Contract: declarations and calls , conditionals , and faults .
import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn positive(value: Int) -> Int: if value > 0: return value else: panic(message: "positive value required") fn discard(value: Int) -> Unit: assert value > 0 test "return contracts": assert positive(value: 3) == 3 discard(value: 1)The faulting branch has no normal successor. discard accepts normal fallthrough because it returns Unit.
Independent variant Expected outcome Remove the else branch in positive Type rejection: a reachable path falls through a non-Unit function Replace if value > 0 with if value Type rejection: condition must be Bool Replace return value with return true Type rejection: returned value is not Int Replace discard’s body with return 1 Type rejection: Int result in a Unit function Replace it with return or return unit Accept: explicit Unit return, like fallthrough Unreachable statements must still parse, resolve, and type-check; they do not repair a missing return on a reachable path.
CL-07: Alternatives, positional payload patterns, and exhaustiveness# Contract: alternatives and pattern matching .
type Outcome: case Ready(value: Int) case Failed(reason: String) fn score(outcome: Outcome) -> Int: match outcome: Ready(value): return value Failed(_): return 0 test "alternative result": assert score(outcome: Outcome.Ready(value: 8)) == 8 assert score(outcome: Outcome.Failed(reason: "unavailable")) == 0Constructors name payload fields; payload patterns bind positions in declaration order. Matching has no fallthrough.
Independent variant Expected outcome Remove Failed arm Type rejection: non-exhaustive match Add another Ready(other) arm Type rejection: duplicate/unreachable arm Replace Ready(value) with Ready(value, extra) Type rejection: payload arity mismatch Replace Ready(value) with Ready(value: local) Parse rejection: payload patterns are positional, not named-call syntax Use Outcome.Ready(amount: 8) in the constructor Type rejection: wrong payload field name Add a final _: arm instead of Failed Accept; wildcard covers the remaining case Add _: with body return 0 after both existing arms Type rejection: every case is already covered, so the wildcard is unreachable Add ambiguity fixtures with two visible alternative types declaring Ready: unqualified construction must be rejected at resolution even when an expected result type could identify one; qualified construction succeeds. Match-case lookup is governed by the scrutinee type.
CL-08: Iteration and nearest-loop control flow# Contract: loops .
import List from "@std/collections.ms" fn selected_sum(values: List[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: if value == 0: continue if value < 0: break total = total + value return total test "iteration control": assert selected_sum(values: [2, 0, 3, -1, 9]) == 5 assert selected_sum(values: []) == 0 Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the iterable values with 3 Type rejection: Int is not an admitted iterable Assign value = 4 in the loop body Type rejection: iteration binding is immutable Put break in the test body outside a loop Type rejection: no enclosing loop Put continue inside a nested anonymous function without its own loop Type rejection: loop control cannot cross a function boundary For nested loops, verify that break and continue select the nearest enclosing loop. For while, verify that the condition is reevaluated and must have type Bool.
CL-09: Generic declaration, inference, and bounds# Contract: generics and equality .
type Box[T: Shareable]: value: T fn unwrap[T: Shareable](box: Box[T]) -> T: return box.value fn same[T: Shareable & Equal](left: T, right: T) -> Bool: return left == right test "generic argument inference": let box = Box[Int](value: 6) assert unwrap(box: box) == 6 assert unwrap[Int](box: box) == 6 assert same(left: 6, right: 6)Inference uses independently typed supplied arguments. Explicit and inferred applications must select the same substitution. Generic bodies are checked against declared bounds, not only the concrete types used by these tests.
Independent variant Expected outcome Use Box[Int, String](value: 6) Type rejection: generic arity mismatch Use Box[String](value: 6) Type rejection: field is not the substituted String type Use unwrap[String](box: box) Type rejection: invariant Box[Int] is not Box[String] Use same(left: 6, right: 6.0) Type rejection: supplied types do not yield one exact T Remove Equal from same’s bound Type rejection in generic body: T does not establish equality Use the undeclared type parameter U in Box’s field Resolution rejection: unknown type U Separate fixture:
import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" fn absent[T: Shareable]() -> Optional[T]: return none test "result context does not infer function arguments": let value: Optional[Int] = absent[Int]()Accept the explicit call. Replacing absent[Int]() with absent() is a type rejection: result context cannot infer a generic function’s type arguments. An expected constructor payload type may provide context for none or an empty list without introducing result-context function inference.
Intrinsic-name rejection fixture:
type Box[Int]: value: IntReject at resolution: a type parameter cannot redefine the intrinsic Int identity. Int is a resolved name rather than a lexical keyword, so this is not a grammar rejection. Apply the same namespace check to module declarations/imports and fixed compiler-bound names, without prohibiting ordinary local shadowing where the module rules permit it.
CL-10: Explicit implementations and contract conversion# Contract: operation contracts .
interface Increment: fn apply(value: Int) -> Int type Offset: delta: Int impl Increment for Offset: fn apply(value: Int) -> Int: return value + self.delta fn use_increment(operation: Increment) -> Int: return operation.apply(value: 4) test "explicit contract conversion": let offset = Offset(delta: 1) let operation = Increment(value: offset) let same_view = Increment(value: operation) assert use_increment(operation: same_view) == 5self is implicit in the implementation body, never a source call argument. Conversion retains the concrete value; applying the same view constructor to an existing exact contract value is an identity conversion. The contract cannot be constructed without a value providing its declared implementation or already having that exact contract type.
Independent variant Expected outcome Pass offset directly as operation Type rejection: conversion to the contract must be explicit Remove the impl declaration Type rejection at conversion: Offset does not implement Increment Rename implementation parameter/body binding from value to item Type rejection: operation labels do not match the contract Change implementation result/body to Float/return 1.0 Type rejection: result signature mismatch Add self: Offset to the implementation parameter list Parse rejection: reserved self cannot be declared as a parameter Repeat the same impl Increment for Offset declaration Type rejection: duplicate implementation Replace Increment(value: offset) with Increment() Type rejection: conversion requires the concrete value argument Add a multi-module rejection fixture for an implementation outside the concrete type’s defining module; path/import mechanics follow module conformance . Contract method ambiguity on a concrete value is resolved by explicit conversion to the selected contract.
CL-10a: Generic implementations and nonoverlap# Contract: generic implementations .
interface ReadValue[T]: fn get() -> T interface SameValue[T: Equal]: fn same(other: T) -> Bool type Box[T]: value: T impl ReadValue[T] for Box[T]: fn get() -> T: return self.value impl SameValue[T] for Box[T]: fn same(other: T) -> Bool: return self.value == other fn compare[T: Equal](box: Box[T], other: T) -> Bool: return box.same(other: other) test "generic implementations": let number = Box[Int](value: 7) let text = Box[String](value: "hello") let number_view = ReadValue[Int](value: number) let text_view = ReadValue[String](value: text) assert number_view.get() == 7 assert text_view.get() == "hello" assert compare(box: number, other: 7) assert not compare(box: number, other: 8)The first block needs no bound to read and return its field. The second inherits Equal from the SameValue interface to compare it. compare proves that implementation’s availability while checking its generic body, without waiting for a concrete instantiation.
Independent variant Expected outcome Add a concrete impl ReadValue[Int] for Box[Int] supplying get() -> Int Type rejection at declaration: overlap with the generic block, even if the body is identical Add another impl ReadValue[T] for Box[T] supplying get() -> T Type rejection at declaration: bounds cannot distinguish overlapping blocks Replace the first block’s ReadValue[T] with ReadValue[Int] Type rejection at declaration: get() -> T does not match the substituted contract result Int Remove Equal from SameValue’s interface parameters Type rejection at declaration: unconstrained field values cannot be compared Remove Equal from compare’s parameters Type rejection in the generic function body: the implementation’s bound is not proved Replace the first block’s receiver Box[T] with bare T Type rejection at declaration: receiver must have a defining nominal data declaration Add [U] to an implementation method Parse rejection: methods cannot introduce their own parameters Also accept disjoint concrete implementations for different receiver applications when no generic block covers them, and two different contract applications for one receiver. For the latter, use explicit views to disambiguate equal operation names. Reject expanding recursive implementation specialization under the ordinary finite-application check. The defining-module rule applies equally to concrete and generic blocks.
CL-10b: Plain and shared contract views# Contract: shared contract views and sharing .
import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" interface ReadValue[T]: fn get() -> T type Box[T]: value: T type SharedReader: reader: ReadValue[Int] & Shareable type CallbackReader: read_value: fn() -> Int impl ReadValue[T] for Box[T]: fn get() -> T: return self.value impl ReadValue[Int] for CallbackReader: fn get() -> Int: return self.read_value() fn seven() -> Int: return 7 fn local_view[T: ReadValue[Int]](source: T) -> ReadValue[Int]: return ReadValue[Int](value: source) fn shared_view[T: ReadValue[Int] & Shareable](source: T) -> ReadValue[Int] & Shareable: return (ReadValue[Int] & Shareable)(value: source) fn consume_shared[T: ReadValue[Int] & Shareable](source: T) -> Int: return source.get() test "plain and shared views": let box = Box[Int](value: 7) let plain = local_view(source: box) let shared = shared_view(source: box) let identity = (ReadValue[Int] & Shareable)(value: shared) let erased = ReadValue[Int](value: identity) let holder = SharedReader(reader: identity) let readers: List[ReadValue[Int] & Shareable] = [holder.reader] let optional: Optional[ReadValue[Int] & Shareable] = some(value: shared) let callback = CallbackReader(read_value: seven) let local_callback = ReadValue[Int](value: callback) assert plain.get() == 7 assert erased.get() == 7 assert local_callback.get() == 7 assert consume_shared(source: holder.reader) == 7local_view must be accepted with no sharing bound on its generic receiver. shared_view retains its proof through the returned type and the record field; the same implementation supplies every view. CallbackReader’s bare function field carries no callable-sharing promise, so the record is nonshareable even though this particular initializer is a safe named function. Its plain view and sequential call are accepted. View conversion evaluates the receiver once and neither copies nor closes native state. The collection and optional declarations exercise refined types inside generic arguments.
Independent variant Expected outcome Remove Shareable from shared_view’s generic bound Type rejection in its body: receiver sharing is not proved Construct (ReadValue[Int] & Shareable)(value: plain) or use erased instead Type rejection: a plain view cannot recover its hidden receiver’s sharing guarantee Replace the callback’s plain view constructor with (ReadValue[Int] & Shareable)(value: callback) Type rejection: the bare function field gives its receiver no sharing proof Pass plain to consume_shared Type rejection at the generic application: named contract bound holds, sharing bound does not Change the list to List[ReadValue[Int]] = [plain] Type rejection: plain contract type fails the collection element bound Initialize SharedReader(reader: plain) Type rejection: plain and shared field types differ Replace ReadValue[Int](value: identity) with identity Accepted: the inferred local retains the shared type rather than erasing it Annotate that replacement as let erased: ReadValue[Int] = identity Type rejection: discarding sharing is not implicit Replace the shared constructor in shared_view with ReadValue[Int](value: source) Type rejection at return: expected shared type cannot refine a plain constructor Replace ReadValue[Int] & Shareable in the record field with Int & Shareable Type rejection: only an operation contract can have this refinement Replace the field type with Shareable & ReadValue[Int] Parse rejection: reversed order is not a value-type form Replace the field type with ReadValue[Int] & Equal Parse rejection: only the Shareable refinement is admitted With a trusted native nonshareable receiver fixture, accept a plain view and sequential calls, reject its shared view construction, and reject concurrently used closures retaining its plain view or bound method. A shared receiver’s method supplies receiver-sharing proof, subject to the existing callable-boundary rules. Verify that a shared service may return a nonshareable local result without making that result shareable. These checks must use frontend proofs rather than Go interface assignability or runtime receiver inspection.
CL-11: Recursive records require immutable-container indirection# Contract: records and generics .
import List from "@std/collections.ms" type Tree[T: Shareable]: value: T children: List[Tree[T]] test "recursive immutable collection": let leaf = Tree[Int](value: 1, children: []) let root = Tree[Int](value: 2, children: [leaf]) assert root.value == 2Accept: removing the List storage edge leaves no inline record/alternative cycle, and recursive applications preserve T unchanged.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the children field type with Tree[T] Type rejection at declaration: unguarded inline cycle Replace it with Optional[Tree[T]] Type rejection at declaration: Optional does not provide storage indirection Replace it with Result[Tree[T], String] Type rejection at declaration: Result does not provide storage indirection Replace it with List[Tree[List[T]]] Type rejection at declaration: recursive application expands the type parameter The declaration check must reject the offending type before constructor errors in the test obscure the cycle. Mutual-recursion fixtures within one module must apply the same graph rule across every participating record/alternative. An import cycle is a separate module rejection, not a substitute for the inline-layout check.
CL-12: Collection iteration has concrete element types# Contract: loops and collections .
import Map from "@std/collections.ms" import MapEntry from "@std/collections.ms" import Set from "@std/collections.ms" fn map_total(values: Map[String, Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for entry in values: let {key, value} = entry let label: String = key total = total + value return total fn set_total(values: Set[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return total test "map entry type": let entry = MapEntry[String, Int](key: "a", value: 3) assert entry.key == "a" assert entry.value == 3Accept these functions with the minimum collection API . The map loop element is MapEntry[String, Int], whose record fields are key: String and value: Int; the set loop element is Int.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace map-loop entry with [key, value] Parse rejection: a loop introduces one identifier, not a destructuring pattern Bind {missing} from entry Type rejection: unknown map-entry record field Declare let label: Int = key Type rejection: map key is String, not Int Replace Set[Int] with Set[Float] Type rejection: Float is not Hashable Replace Map[String, Int] with Map[List[Int], Int] Type rejection: collections are not hashable keys Runtime collection fixtures use the minimum constructor/update API: verify insertion-order traversal for maps and sets, and evaluate an effectful iterable expression exactly once. The concrete expectations are in runtime bindings .
CL-13: Lexical text forms and declaration-only modules# Contract: source grammar and text .
fn echo(value: String) -> String: return value test "text source forms": assert echo(value: "\{literal\}") == "\{literal\}" assert "\u{1F600}" == "😀" assert "value: {3}" == "value: 3" let no_value: Unit = unitEscaped braces are literal text; unescaped braces select interpolation. Source UTF-8 encoding and Unicode scalar validation are part of parsing text, independent of later text-conversion APIs.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the scalar escape with "\u{D800}" Parse rejection: surrogate is not a Unicode scalar Replace it with "\u{110000}" Parse rejection: scalar exceeds the Unicode range Replace an escape with "\q" Parse rejection: unknown escape Replace echo’s function name with the reserved word if Parse rejection: reserved word is not an identifier Add module-level let extra = 1 after the test Parse rejection: executable bindings belong in a block Replace let no_value: Unit = unit with let no_value: Unit = 0 Type rejection: Int is not Unit Replace it with let smallest: Int = -9223372036854775808 Accept: directly negated minimum Int literal Replace it with let too_large = 9223372036854775808 Type rejection: positive literal is outside Int range Replace it with let too_large = 1e400 Type rejection: Float literal would round to infinity Replace it with let unknown = 01 Parse rejection: leading-zero numeric spelling is not supported Equivalent LF and CRLF encodings must produce the same parsed structure after documented newline normalization. Invalid UTF-8 input must be rejected rather than silently replaced. Blank/comment-only lines do not introduce suites, and comment markers within text remain text.
CL-14: Result propagation preserves the declared error type# Contract: Result and try propagation .
import Result from "@std/result.ms" type Problem: case Missing(reason: String) type OtherProblem: case Invalid(reason: String) fn checked(value: Int) -> Result[Int, Problem]: if value < 0: return error(cause: Problem.Missing(reason: "negative")) return ok(value: value) fn doubled(value: Int) -> Result[Int, Problem]: let accepted = try checked(value: value) return ok(value: accepted * 2) fn summarize(outcome: Result[Int, Problem]) -> Int: match outcome: ok(value): return value error(_): return -1 test "unchanged propagated error": assert summarize(outcome: doubled(value: 3)) == 6 assert summarize(outcome: doubled(value: -1)) == -1Successful construction obtains the complete Result[Int, Problem] type from the declared return contract. Propagation leaves the remaining body unexecuted on an expected error; it does not introduce an implicit error union or conversion.
Independent variant Expected outcome Change only doubled’s declared error type to OtherProblem Type rejection at try: incompatible propagated error Change doubled to return Int, and its final return to return accepted * 2 Type rejection at try: enclosing function must return compatible Result Replace ok(value: value) with ok(value: true) Type rejection: wrong successful payload type Replace the error payload with OtherProblem.Invalid(reason: "negative") Type rejection: wrong declared error payload type Replace the try operand with value Type rejection: operand is not Result Replace the local binding with let accepted: Int = try ok(value: 3) Type rejection: annotation does not propagate through try to infer the missing error type Replace the local binding with let accepted = try Result[Int, Problem].ok(value: value) Accept: qualification establishes both Result arguments before propagation An anonymous function establishes its own propagation boundary. Test that an inner Unit closure cannot use try merely because its enclosing function returns Result; the inner function’s signature controls compatibility.
CL-15: Equality eligibility does not imply hashing eligibility# Contract: equality and hashing .
import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Decimal from "@std/decimal.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" type Callback: handler: fn(value: Int) -> Int fn increment(value: Int) -> Int: return value + 1 fn preserve_key[K: Hashable](value: K) -> K: return value test "derived value equality": let present: Optional[Int] = some(value: 1) let same: Optional[Int] = some(value: 1) let missing: Optional[Int] = none assert present == same assert present != missing assert 1.00d == 1d assert [1, 2] == [1, 2] assert [1, 2] != [2, 1] assert preserve_key(value: "key") == "key" let callback = Callback(handler: increment)Optional equality compares its tag and eligible payload. Decimal equality compares numeric values despite different trailing zeroes. List equality observes positions rather than treating a list as a set. Eligibility is checked recursively on record fields.
Independent variant Expected outcome Add assert callback == callback Type rejection: a function field makes Callback ineligible for equality Add assert increment == increment Type rejection: function values have no equality Use preserve_key(value: [1, 2]) Type rejection: equal lists are not hashable Use preserve_key(value: 1.0) Type rejection: Float is equal-comparable but not hashable Declare let wrong: Optional[Float] = present Type rejection: invariant optional applications differ Test generated record/alternative equality with eligible scalar leaves and reject derivations containing a noneligible leaf. Do not treat sharing eligibility, identical object references, or a user-written marker implementation as evidence of equality.
CL-16: Expected data types supply constructor context# Contract: compatibility and expected types , Optional , and Result .
import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" type Input: names: List[Optional[String]] fn outcome_value(outcome: Result[Int, String]) -> Int: match outcome: ok(value): return value error(_): return -1 test "data constructor context": let input = Input(names: [none, some(value: "Ada")]) let success: Result[Int, String] = ok(value: 3) let failure: Result[Int, String] = error(cause: "unavailable") let absent: Optional[Int] = none let nested: List[List[Int]] = [[], [1]] assert outcome_value(outcome: success) == 3 assert outcome_value(outcome: failure) == -1The field, binding annotation, or substituted parameter determines missing data arguments; it does not convert an independently known incompatible type. Forward declarations and contextual list elements do not require module-level execution.
Independent variant Expected outcome Remove : Result[Int, String] from success Type rejection: ok’s payload does not determine the error type Remove it from failure Type rejection: error’s payload does not determine the success type Remove : Optional[Int] from absent Type rejection: none supplies no payload type Change some(value: "Ada") to some(value: 3) Type rejection: independently known payload conflicts with expected String Replace none for absent with 3 Type rejection: no implicit Optional wrapping Replace ok(value: 3) for success with 3 Type rejection: no implicit Result wrapping Add a nonempty-list fixture [none, some(value: 1)]: the independently typed some determines Optional[Int] for the absent element. Reject [some(value: 1), some(value: "one")]; no implicit union is formed. These data-constructor rules do not infer a missing generic function specialization from its result context; CL-09 checks that separate boundary.
CL-17: Nonreturning subexpressions determine control-flow exits# Contract: Unit and Never .
The following independent module is a type-checking fixture; its faulting functions are not invoked as passing tests.
import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn failed_initializer() -> Never: let impossible: Int = panic(message: "initializer cannot return") fn returned_failure() -> Int: return panic(message: "result cannot return") fn endless() -> Int: while true: assert trueAccept: the initializer and return expression cannot produce values; the literal-true loop has no reachable break and therefore no normal exit. An expected annotation does not make a Never expression return an Int at runtime.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the initializer with 0 Type rejection: the Never function now reaches normal fallthrough Replace the binding with let impossible: Int = 1 + panic(message: "stop") Accept: the operator result is Int, but its required right operand cannot return Replace the binding with let impossible: Bool = not panic(message: "stop") Accept: not selects Bool, but its required operand cannot return Replace the binding with let impossible: Int = panic(message: "left") + panic(message: "right") Type rejection: two Never operands supply no numeric candidate, even under an Int annotation Replace the binding with let impossible: Int = -panic(message: "stop") Type rejection: unary numeric selection requires an independently known numeric operand Replace the binding with let possible: Bool = false and panic(message: "skipped") Type rejection: the Never function has reachable fallthrough because the right operand is skipped Replace the binding with let possible: Bool = true or panic(message: "skipped") Type rejection: short circuiting permits normal fallthrough Add return unit after its initializer Type rejection: unreachable returns still must match the declared result type Replace return panic(...) with bare return Type rejection: a non-Unit function requires a value Replace while true with while not false Type rejection: nonliteral conditions retain a possible exit; no constant folding proves return completeness Add a reachable break inside endless Type rejection: the loop can exit and the Int function then falls through Extend the fixture with a nested loop whose own break does not exit the outer literal-true loop. A closure’s return likewise does not return from its enclosing function. Nonreturning callable/argument evaluation prevents later arguments and the outer call from running, under the ordinary evaluation-order contract.
CL-18: Suite-bodied function expressions resume the enclosing layout# Contract: anonymous-function suites and function values .
import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn apply(value: Int, transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int) -> Int: return transform(value: value) test "function suite boundaries": let dormant = fn() -> Int: return panic(message: "body is not run at creation") let grouped = apply( transform: ( fn(value: Int) -> Int: if value > 0: return value - 1 return 0 ), value: 3, ) let final_argument = apply( value: 3, transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int: return value - 1 ) assert grouped == 2 assert final_argument == 2The unused closure’s body must not run. Its dedent terminates both the function expression and the surrounding binding statement, so the next binding does not require an extra blank line. The grouped closure ends before the outer argument comma; the final ungrouped closure resumes the still-open call’s continuation when its body dedents. The nested if dedents within the active function suite rather than ending the enclosing call.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace dormant’s function expression with fn() -> Int: 1 Parse rejection: a function body requires a statement suite Indent the final call-closing ) to the closure-body level Parse rejection: a delimiter opened outside the function body cannot close at body indentation Add let after = 1 at the next test-body indentation without a blank line after dormant Accept: synthetic statement boundary follows the function-expression suite Replace the anonymous expression with a nested named fn dormant() -> Int: declaration Parse rejection: named functions are not local statements Coverage and evidence# Maintain one independently checked fixture for each accepted module and each rejected variant. Record actual compiler results separately from the expected outcomes here. Scalar conversions, collection construction, and numeric edge behavior have runtime acceptance cases .

title: Runtime binding acceptance cases
content:
Runtime binding acceptance cases# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index These design fixtures cover standard API binding, sharing, data, host, and adapter rules alongside core-language conformance . Check each accepted module and rejected mutation independently.
Standard imports and declaration identity# import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Decimal from "@std/decimal.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" fn amount() -> Result[Decimal, String]: return ok(value: 12.50d) test "explicit standard imports": assert [1, 2].length() == 2 let outcome = map_error( result: amount(), transform: fn(cause: String) -> Int: return cause.byte_length() ) match outcome: ok(value): assert value == 12.50d error(_): assert falseAccept without an [aliases] table. Independently remove List and reject its bracket literal; remove Decimal and reject its annotation/literal; remove Result and reject its annotation and expression constructor lookup; remove map_error and reject its call. Importing Result alone must not expose map_error, and importing a function must not expose the type names in its signature. Match cases remain available from an inferred scrutinee even when its type name is not imported, as in the CLI entry fixture .
Accept this independent module without standard imports:
type List: count: Int type Result: case Value(value: Int) fn parallel(value: Int) -> Int: return value fn ordinary() -> Result: return Result.Value(value: parallel(value: 3)) test "standard spellings are ordinary names": assert List(count: 2).count == 2 let forward = parallel assert forward(value: 4) == 4 match ordinary(): Value(value): assert value == 3Adding the canonical List or Result import rejects its collision with the local declaration. try ordinary() is rejected: this Result is not the standard alternative. A bracket literal is rejected without the standard List import even though a local List exists. Calling this local parallel with a tasks pack does not activate the standard binding’s special typing. Extracting the local parallel above is accepted as an ordinary function value. Preserve the imported parallel/parallel_map/Background callable restrictions in all existing sharing fixtures. Independently reject unimported parallel, parallel_map, Background, ExecutionError, OperationId, StartError, and check_cancelled in otherwise well-formed calls or annotations; importing one standard export must not expose the rest. A local check_cancelled function remains an ordinary function and receives no runtime checkpoint behavior.
Module-resolution cases reject an [aliases] entry for @std, @std without a module path, a missing standard file/export, and paths or symlinks escaping the standard-library directory. Resolving a standard module in two installation directories with identical pinned contents preserves identity; changing its pinned distribution invalidates module/analysis/code-generation caches. Adapter interfaces may import standard declarations but cannot use that exception to import application files. Imports alone acquire no external authority.
Error adaptation and inferred packs# import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" fn identity[T](value: T) -> T: return value fn probe() -> Result[Unit, ExecutionError]: let first = fn() -> Result[Int, String]: return ok(value: 3) let second = fn() -> Bool: return true let packed = try parallel(tasks: [first, second]) let copied = identity(value: packed) let [number, flag] = copied assert flag match number: ok(value): assert value == 3 error(_): assert false return ok(value: unit) test "pack helper": match probe(): ok(_): assert true error(_): assert false test "explicit error conversion": let failed: Result[Int, Int] = error(cause: 7) let translate = fn(cause: Int) -> String: return "Error {cause}" let converted = map_error(result: failed, transform: translate) let expected: Result[Int, String] = error(cause: "Error 7") assert converted == expectedAccept the complete load module in parallel too. Replace any error adapter with direct try under LoadError and reject the incompatible error type. Moving the probe’s try parallel directly into the Unit test is rejected. Changing the copied pack pattern to [number] is rejected for arity. Passing an existing list as tasks is rejected; qualifying or annotating a source type Pack is an unknown-name rejection. parallel(tasks: []) can be matched and its success destructured as [].
For mapping, accept fn(item: Int) -> Int and reject an otherwise identical fn(id: Int) -> Int. Reject start operations returning Int or plain Unit; accept only shareable fn() -> Result[Unit, String]. Use controlled reporter fixtures to verify String errors, crashes, status expiry, bounded overflow fallback, and reporter-fault fallback without recursive reporting.
Sharing and contract cleanup# import Bytes from "@std/bytes.ms" import File from "@std/io.ms" import IoError from "@std/io.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" type ClosedFile: marker: Unit impl File for ClosedFile: fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError]: return error(cause: IoError.Closed) fn close() -> Unit: return test "contract-valued cleanup": with file = File(value: ClosedFile(marker: unit)): match file.read(max_bytes: 1): ok(_): assert false error(cause): assert cause == IoError.ClosedThis fake represents an already-closed stream, so its close is idempotent and has no external release obligation. Also accept (File & Shareable)(value: ClosedFile(marker: unit)) as the with initializer: cleanup works with either view. Reject with over a concrete type merely having a method named close without impl Closeable. Reject a contract with the wrong close signature. Verify native and source fake shared File values are interchangeable through Files.open’s Result[File & Shareable, IoError] result.
A bare function parameter carries no sharing proof. Reject a parallel closure capturing that parameter, even if a particular caller passes a safe named function. Accept a plain view over an implementing record containing a bare function field or unsynchronized native state for sequential use, but reject its shared view construction; such storage lacks a type-level sharing guarantee. Accept concurrent captures of shared contract views, shareable concrete receivers, and generic values bounded by both Shareable and the behavioral contract. Reject concurrent captures of plain contract views and bound methods extracted from them, even when a particular runtime receiver is safe.
Test captured-function wrappers and branch/var merges so an unsafe alternative cannot retain a safe callable proof.
Independently reject this complete module at the parallel call: generic forwarding erases the callable proof even for this safe input.
import Result from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" fn identity[T](value: T) -> T: return value fn rejected_forwarding() -> Result[Unit, ExecutionError]: let safe = fn() -> Int: return 1 let forwarded = identity(value: safe) let [value] = try parallel(tasks: [forwarded]) return ok(value: unit)Replacing forwarded with safe accepts the function. A generic function with T: Shareable instead rejects passing safe at bound checking. A Box[T] field storing a function does not restore the erased proof; Box[T: Shareable] rejects a function type argument. Ordinary generic data values and inferred result packs retain their type-level sharing properties; their behavior is unchanged.
Independently reject extracting let launch = background.start, let mapper = parallel_map[Int, Int], let constructor = Background, a bare parallel reference, and forwarding these references to identity or a function parameter. These call-only bindings have requirements a plain function type cannot retain. Accept direct explicitly specialized parallel_map calls with proven-safe callbacks. A source wrapper that accepts an ordinary function parameter and forwards it to Background.start is rejected for missing callable proof at that direct call.
Data and numeric outcomes# Use the accepted modules in minimum data operations . In addition:
import Decimal from "@std/decimal.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" fn quotient(value: Int, divisor: Int) -> Int: return value / divisor fn remainder(value: Int, divisor: Int) -> Int: return value % divisor test "numeric boundary rules": assert quotient(value: -7, divisor: 2) == -3 assert remainder(value: -7, divisor: 3) == -1 assert remainder(value: -9223372036854775808, divisor: -1) == 0 let infinity = 1.0 / 0.0 let nan = 0.0 / 0.0 assert "{infinity}" == "Infinity" assert nan != nan let third = 1d / 3d assert "{third}" == "0.3333333333333333333333333333333333" let absent: Optional[Int] = none assert 1e300.truncate_to_int() == absent assert (2.seconds + 1.seconds) == 3.secondsRunner-level fault probes use parameters for division by zero, minimum Int/-1, unary minimum Int negation, duration overflow, Decimal overflow, and invalid byte construction. Assert normal subnormal/zero Decimal underflow and halfway ties-to-even. Reject out-of-grid Decimal literals and more than 34 significant digits; accept insignificant trailing zeroes. Map mutation tests verify a/b/a-replacement traversal as a→3,b→2, original snapshot retention, and remove/reinsert ordering. Reject source implementations for standard native collection types.
Entry, adapter, and lifetime integration# Build the complete CLI main module with an ms.toml selecting it, pass two arguments, and expect Arguments: 2 plus LF and exit 0. Missing/internal/generic/wrong-signature main must fail checking. Inject SIGINT and SIGTERM during joined work and verify joins/cleanup before exits 130/143. A cleanup fault exits 70. Host escalation is separately classified as incomplete cleanup.
Generate a separate schema package for a minimal interface, a native adapter package importing it, and an application importing both; the pinned Go toolchain must build this without an import cycle. Reject interface imports of an application module, invalid/duplicate bindings, absent acquisition disposers, wrong native symbol signatures, and mutable/invalid foreign result values.
Controlled race probes cover acquisition versus cancellation, completion versus stop, admission versus close, repeated close, and close from an admitted job’s nested parallel descendant or reporter. The latter must fault before shutdown instead of self-joining. Generic function specialization probes accept regular self/mutual recursion and reject expanding specialization through calls or stored function values before Go emission.

title: Semantic conformance tests
content:
Semantic conformance tests# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A conformance test establishes a language guarantee through observable behavior. Concurrency tests need both controlled transitions and stress under real scheduling.
Core-language fixtures specify independent accepted modules and rejected variants for the grammar, operators, inference, contracts, and control flow. Their parse/resolution/type outcomes are authoritative for this core pass; the runtime coverage below remains a separate conformance track.
Tests use test "name": blocks and ordinary assert. Control fake I/O, virtual clocks, and barriers around runtime transitions; Go goroutine scheduling remains nondeterministic. Stress and race tests exercise real transitions. Required coverage includes source-order preparation, exact heterogeneous results, domain errors, snapshot captures, sharing bounds, with registration and cleanup, closed-resource aliases, atomic admission/completion/close races, cleanup faults, and fixed deadline parents.
Test runner# A source test body is checked as a zero-parameter Unit function. Discovery and execution are still unspecified: the runner needs a command, file selection rules, stable test identities, duplicate-name handling, isolation, authority inputs, and a way to expect a programming fault. It must also define whether test bodies enter ordinary builds. The examples here fix expected behavior without assuming those runner decisions.
Tests in source# The parallel API requires coverage for empty, one-position, and heterogeneous literal task packs; source-order preparation; result ordering despite reversed completion; unchanged domain results; and cancellation/fault paths that join all started work. Cover each row of the joining outcome table with a virtual timer: caller cancellation during a group timeout unwinds the caller, a cleanup fault after a timeout reports Crashed, an empty pack with a zero timeout succeeds, and a nonempty pack with a zero timeout reports TimedOut without running any body. Verify that a while loop with no explicit checkpoint unwinds at its next back-edge after cancellation. Reject non-function task entries and functions requiring arguments. Verify that let [resA, resB] = try parallel(tasks: [first, second]) preserves each result’s type inside a helper returning Result[Unit, ExecutionError]; the Unit test matches that helper’s result and asserts success. Direct try parallel(...) in a Unit test is rejected. Mixed domain/execution errors use map_error, as in the complete parallel example.
Destructuring conformance covers array and record patterns, shorthand, renaming, nesting, let and var, and single evaluation of the initializer. Reject parenthesized positional bindings, fixed-pack arity mismatches, unknown fields, and duplicate local names. Check that dynamic list length mismatches fault rather than introducing missing values or discarding extra elements.
Module conformance covers relative, user-alias, and explicit standard imports, the reserved @std alias, standard declaration identity independent of installation path, rejection of missing imports and standard-name collisions, manifest-relative configuration, canonical file identity, project containment after symlink resolution, visibility, and cycle rejection. Check aliases at complete segment boundaries and invalidate cached analysis when relevant configuration changes. Project configuration defines the accepted and rejected paths; external Manuscript dependency projects are unsupported.
Named list-argument conformance covers empty, one-element, and multi-element lists, passing existing lists, multiple list parameters, and calls through function values. Reject unnamed, duplicate, unknown, or missing arguments, incompatible list element types, and nonshareable list elements. Use controlled capability calls to verify left-to-right list-element evaluation and source order between named arguments, including closure creation and with initialization.
test "checked decrement": let value = 3 assert value - 1 > 0This illustrates the test-block syntax and ordinary assertion form. Runtime tests need fake capabilities, virtual clocks, and barriers to arrange meaningful races, rather than assuming a fixed goroutine schedule.
For an acquisition race, verify that the adapter closes a newly acquired resource if delivery loses to cancellation, and that with registers a delivered resource without a cancellation gap. Never recursively close arbitrary parallel result fields or captures. Test aliases invoked after scope exit, concurrent operation/close races, stale pooled leases, reverse close order, and idempotent shutdown. Background tests cover bounded rejection, closed admission, independent siblings, observed domain errors and faults, bounded reporting state, optional drain, cancellation, and joining. A captured var keeps its creation-time value; assignment to an outer captured local is rejected.
See completion and acquisition and complete-program evidence .

title: Complete-program conformance
content:
Complete-program conformance# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Individual semantic checks must also hold together in complete programs. These programs connect scoped cleanup, concurrency, external I/O, and tooling.
Validate these complete programs as their APIs become concrete:
Program Required evidence CLI argument output and bounded file reads exact Process entry, explicit authority, specified stream signatures, cleanup, and exit behavior CLI draining subprocess stdout/stderr concurrent streaming and deterministic resource release Bounded HTTP server with slow clients admission, backpressure, limits, failure isolation Background worker surviving a submitting helper’s completion fixed service parent, bounded admission, error observation, and joined shutdown Cancellation during resource acquisition atomic completion and disposal of undelivered resources Nested cleanup with a fault every remaining cleanup runs exactly once; secondary diagnostics retained Debug session through parallel, Background, and with source stepping, value rendering, and task inspection Fixture contents# Each fixture includes complete source, ms.toml, adapter inputs, arguments and environment, and an expected transcript and exit outcome. Race fixtures also specify controlled barriers, allowed outcomes, and which resources must be released. Debug fixtures specify source stops and the values visible at each stop. A scenario description alone is not executable evidence.
The subprocess, HTTP, and debugger fixtures depend on the outstanding API and tooling decisions .
See semantic coverage and implementation priorities .

title: Scope and implementation order
content:
Scope and implementation order# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Implementation order follows the dependencies between the language, library, runtime, compiler, and tooling.
Implementation order# Parse and check the language, including named calls, exact types, contracts, captures, and sharing. Implement lexical cleanup and atomic start, cancellation, completion, and close transitions together. Connect standard imports, data operations, CLI host, streams, and adapters; validate complete programs. Complete the queue, pool, builder, HTTP, and subprocess APIs using the same lifetime and cancellation rules. Build source tools, diagrams, traces, and debugging on checked compiler facts and matching runtime metadata. Use the semantic tests and complete programs to check that these parts agree. A written acceptance case becomes evidence only when an implementation runs it and records the result.
Outstanding decisions# These gaps still need concrete contracts.
Area Details still needed Authoritative page Test runner Discovery, test identity, duplicate names, isolation, authority inputs, expected faults, and build inclusion Semantic tests Build distribution External adapter/dependency locks and supported debugger distribution Reproducibility Native adapter ABI Generated Go declarations, receiver construction, disposer types, and compatibility validation Adapter manifests Capability analysis Classification of adapter interfaces, pure contracts, wrappers, and indirect authority Authority Queue extensions Fairness and additional channel patterns beyond the bounded FIFO contract Queues State and pool extensions Atomic update APIs, native resource factories, and additional lease contracts State and pools Builder extensions Additional bulk mutation operations beyond sealed snapshot construction Builders HTTP and subprocess extensions Streaming, sessions, HTTP clients, and platform descendant supervision HTTP hosts , streams Source tools Rich diagnostic spans, transactional structural edits, and failed-write recovery Source tools Diagrams and debugging Stable node identity, diff/trace formats, stepping behavior, value rendering, and supported debugger versions Developer tooling For each gap, add exact signatures or data fields, success and failure behavior, an accepted example, and a boundary or rejected example to its concept page. Then add observable conformance expectations. Other guides should link to the rule rather than repeat it.
Unsupported features# Actors, detached tasks, task adoption, racing combinators, inheritance, macros, operator overloading, implicit conversions, and user-defined metaprogramming have no supported forms. More specific syntax exclusions appear on the relevant concept pages.
Forced task termination is unsupported. Uncooperative work can delay joining indefinitely; host escalation is an incomplete shutdown, not successful cleanup. See cancellation and background shutdown .

title: Developer tooling
content:

Diagrams and traces # System, flow, and detail views Reading a concurrent-flow diagram Architecture diffs Execution traces and overlays 3.
